subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 91 respecting banks and banking.
* He said: Mr. Speaker, I think I should give a very brief explanation on the first reading.
This bill is intended to constitute the basis of the decennial revision of the Bank Act. It extends the charters of the existing ten chartered banks for another ten-year period, in other words, until July 1, 1954. In addition, it provides for a great many changes in the 'resent legislation governing the operations if the banks, their powers and the limitations *hd controls to which they are subject.
Several of these changes are not only important but complicated, and some of them tie in with other legislation to be introduced at this session. I intend to make an extended statement on second reading in order to give the house as clear and complete an explanation as possible of these changes, as well as of the philosophy and guiding principles with which we approached this revision of our banking legislation. At the present time all I will do is to call attention to the more important changes we are recommending.
These changes may be listed as follows:
(1)	Changes regarding note issue, to be found in sections 60 and 61, taking away the right of a bank to issue or reissue notes in Canada after January 1, 1945, and providing for the complete retirement of such notes after January I, 1950. Right to issue outside of Canada is limited to ten per cent of paid up capital, and there are a number of consequential provisions.

(2)	Various provisions making the Bank of Canada the exclusive agency for redemption of notes, both of defunct banks and, by 1950, of the existing banks.
(3)	An amendment to section 92 to provide for transfer of unclaimed deposits,. et cetera, and the liability to repay them, to the Bank of Canada-after ten years.
(4)	Amendments to section 91, reducing the maximum rate of interest or discount which banks may charge from seven to six per cent, and allowing banks to make unsecured personal instalment loans on a basis equivalent to a five per cent discount for a one-year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments.
(5)	Various amendments to make it possible for additional types of borrowers to get credit under section 88.
(6)	Suggested amendments proposed for the consideration of the banking and commerce committee to simplify the complicated procedure now necessary in connection with section 88 loans.
_ (7) Various important amendments to sections 88 and 89 in order enable the banks to meet the special needs of farmers and fishermen, chiefly for intermediate credit. These provisions are to be, supplemented by other legislation, which I shall explain to the house on second reading of this bill.

It is a bulky volume, and anybody who intends to give any study to this bill should be given time to do so, notwithstanding what is no doubt the desire on all sides to have the bill referred to the banking and commerce committee at as early a day as possible. But I suggest to the minister that twenty-four hours is not enough time, and we might arrange by consent that the second reading come up on Thursday, when he will make his statement, if that is convenient and satisfactory to the minister. Before the minister turns down that suggestion, I would point this out to him, if I have the consent of the house. We are now

So that this bill must have been in preparation for a long time, and it is pretty late to be introducing it now. The principle which has always been observed with regard to subsidy payments is that information as to subsidies paid on recent or current business is not revealed, on two or three grounds which I have stated. I am quite content, if any hon. member requests information as to whether a particular dealer or person has received a subsidy, to see that that is answered yes or no, and also to give information as to the principle on which the subsidy is paid to him. subtopic: LOSS OF H.M.C.S. "ATHABASKAN" IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LOSS OF H.M.C.S. "ATHABASKAN" IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL
speechtext:
I should like to make an inquiry of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, notice of which I have given him.
We all read with mingled feelings of pride, admiration and sorrow of the naval action which was fought in the English channel off the French coast in the early hours of last Saturday morning. It was with pride that we learned that His Majesty's Canadian Ship Athabaskan fought back, and gave as good as she got until she was split in two by an enemy torpedo, and sank.
Our admiration was roused by the brave unselfishness of Lieutenant Commander Stubbs, D.S.O., of Victoria, B.C., who gallantly chose to risk death himself in order to save the crew of the Alhabaskan's sister ship, H.M.C.S. Haida, which later exacted quick revenge by driving one of the German destroyers ashore in flames. Coupled with the name of Lieutenant Commander Stubbs must be mentioned Commander H. G. De Wolf, of the Royal Canadian-Navy, of Halifax, commander of the Haida, whose coolness and daring was responsible for the rescue of many of the Athabaskan's crew. I have learned since that on the Haida was the son of the late lamented Hugh B. McKinnon, who was such an honoured member of the present House of Commons.
Canadian people heard with sorrow in their hearts the news of the brave lads who lost their lives in this further bright page in the valorous narrative of our new but powerful navy, of which every citizen in Canada is so justly proud.
I have taken the liberty of making these observations as a preliminary to a question which I desire to direct to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Is the minister in a position, within the limits of security, to give the house any further details of this action beyond those which have appeared up to the present in the press?
2492'
Loss of H.M.C.S. Athabaskan

Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend the leader of the opposition for his references, which I am sure are concurred in by every hon. member of this house. Certainly I myself share most genuinely his pride in the conduct of the Athabaskan's officers and men and his sorrow for those -who have given their lives.
We do not know and we shall not know for some time how many men have been lost and how many have been made prisoners of war. The direct question which my hon. friend put to me as to further details of the action beyond those which have appeared already in the press is one that perhaps I cannot answer properly at the moment, because I am not sure that I have anything to add to what has already been given to the public either in the press or on the radio. I can however give to the house a summary of the dispatches received at naval service headquarters.
During an offensive sweep in the English channel early on Saturday, April 29, 1944, licht forces of the Royal Canadian Navy encountered two enemy destroyers of the Elbing class in the vicinity of the He de Vierge near TJshant. The Canadian ships were:	His
Majesty's Canadian Ship Haida, under Commander H. G. de Wolf, R.C.N., and His Majesty's Canadian Ship Athabaskan, under Lieutenant-Commander J. H. Stubbs, D.S.O., R.C.N. Our ships immediately opened fire, to which the enemy replied with heavy and accurate fire. The Athabaskan w'as hit twice by shells, but continued firing until she was .struck by an enemy torpedo and sunk.
Repeated hits were obtained by our ships on the enemy, and one of the enemy shipsw'as driven ashore in flames. The remaining enemy destroyer escaped in the smoke and darkness. The action was continued to within close distance of enemy-occupied territory.
As to survivors:	One officer and thirteen
ratings, .whose injuries are not serious, are at present in the Royal Naval hospital, Plymouth, England. Six ratings, whose injuries are also not considered to be serious, are in the West Cornwall hospital, Penzance, Cornwall, England. One rating, slightly injured, is in the Royal Naval barracks, Devenport, England. Twenty-five ratings are also in the Royal Naval barracks at Devenport. That makes a total of forty-six of the Athabaskan complement that we know to be in England. Of that number one officer and thirty-nine ratings were picked up by the Canadian ship Haida, and the remaining six ratings made their way to the south coast of England in a motor boat dropped by the Haida before leaving the scene. The Haida [DOT]dropped other boats and rafts. It is reported

by the German radio that eighty-five prisoners, including six officers, were taken from the water and are now in German hands.
The next-of-kin of casualties are being informed as soon as possible. I am glad to say that there were no casualties whatever in the Canadian ship Haida, which returned safely *to port.

subtopic: LOSS OF H.M.C.S. "ATHABASKAN" IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL
speechtext: We associate ourselves with the remarks of the leader of the opposition. Does the procedure that has been followed in this case mean that a new policy has been adopted and that the loss of ships and so on will be announced before the relatives have.been informed as to casualties? I am sure we all sympathize with the relatives of the men in their period of anxiety and uncertainty. I thought the policy was that the announcement of losses would be made after the relatives had been notified of casualties. It seems to me that is the policy that should be pursued. When I heard the announcement on the air at noon yesterday I felt much disturbed because of the anxiety that I knew would prevail in a large number of Canadian homes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: LOSS OF H.M.C.S. "ATHABASKAN" IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, the policy has been and still is to inform the next of kin of any casualties before any public announcement is made. But in this case, as I am sure many hon. members of the house know', announcements began to come over the German radio as early as Saturday to the effect that they had sunk a ship and that they had a certain number of prisoners; consequently it was felt that the only thing that could be done here and in Britain was that an announcement should be made by ourselves, giving such information as we had, meagre and sketchy though it might be. Furthermore, as to these men who are prisoners of war, my hon. friend will realize that it will be some time before those names are available. Often it takes as long as three months for this government to be informed of the identity of war prisoners. As my hon. friend undoubtedly knows, this information comes from the Red Cross. It would be necessary for us to make some announcement before the end of three months in any event, and our announcement would consequently have to be made before we had full particulars as to survivors.

In addition twenty-six preserve coupons will be available each of which can be used either for the purchase of one-half pound of sugar or varying quantities of sweet spreads or canned fruit. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, April 28, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
. DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
National selective service programme, $11,002,429.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to the address of the minister on Friday last, I wish to accept his summing up, as found on page 2447 of Hansard, of the task of selective service during the coming months. He said that the major task of the selective service system over the next few months will be:
First, to provide the required men for the armed services; second, to meet the labour needs of agriculture; third, to place in employment men discharged from the armed forces; fourth, to meet, as they develop, the urgent needs of certain key industries; fifth, to place men laid off as a result of changes in munition production schedules as quickly and efficiently as possible.
At the outset I wish to commend the Minister of Labour for the very full report he has given. His courtesy and willingness to furnish information deserve the highest praise. With some of the statistics he has given us I am not in agreement, but I do appreciate, as I am sure the committee does, the fact that the Minister of Labour is always willing to place before the house and the country the situation as he sees it. He claims that selective service
War Appropriation-Labour

has been very successful, but with that point of view I am not in complete agreement. I believe that the work being done by selective service in placing the men returning from overseas and those discharged in Canada has been most successful.
In that regard, I should like to ascertain what machinery has been set up to assist in the delhobilization of the armed forces, and to assure them of work. What about the men who since the beginning of the war have been employed in war plants that are to Be shut down? What about the men who joined the armed forces from munitions plants that will be closed down when they return from overseas? What provision will be made to assure these men of employment? What about the thirty thousand men who were not employed before they joined the armed services? The British government has announced its plan, under which the order of demobilization will depend upon age and length of service, with preference of course being given to service overseas. The local employment office here in Ottawa has done a particularly good job in a survey it made with a view to ascertaining whether jobs will be available when the war is over, and the order in which those jobs will become available. According to the information I have been given, the Ottawa employment office made a survey of 57-8 per cent of all war-time A and B priority industries in this area in order to ascertain how the industrial structure has been changed and whether after the war the demand and supply in connection with workers will be near balance. They found that as far as A priority industries are concerned, 6-6 per cent of the men will be released immediately upon termination of the war contracts; 37 per cent will be released one month later, 45 per cent three months later and 40 per cent six months later. In other words a vast army of men will be discharged from class A industries within a period of six months after the termination of their war contracts. So far as B priority industries are concerned, 2-4 per cent of the men will be released on the termination of war contracts, 3-7 per cent one month later, 4-7 per cent three months later and 6-5 per cent six months later. This means that hundreds of thousands of men and women now employed in A and B priority industries will be released within a few months after the end of the war. What about the employment of these people? I understand a survey has been made by the industrial mobilization survey board for the purpose of ascertaining how many positions will be available, and how many men can be combed out of industry for military service.
I think we should have a report by the 
minister on the result of that survey. How many men may expect to be combed out of industry within the next sixty days under the findings arrived at by this organization?
There can be no disagreement in this house, of course, with the commendation expressed by the minister of the men and women in the armed services, and I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house will concur in his remarks concerning the contribution to the war effort made by the women of Canada. We have 235,000 women in industry, in addition to thousands in the armed forces and the hundreds of thousands in their own households, engaged in patriotic work and doing their part in sacrifice and service.
Now, however, I come to a phase in connection with which there is some disagreement. I accept as a premise in connection with the operation of selective service, and I do not think it can be denied, that the foundation of unity in Canada depends upon equality of sacrifice and equality under the law without regard to any outside considerations whatsoever. We have declared for total war, but total war is impossible unless there is full partnership between our citizens, both military and civilian; and there can be no unity in this country unless there is a willingness and determination on the part of our citizens to serve equally in this war effort. Canadian citizenship is meaningless unless it implies a single standard of duty and responsibility everywhere in this dominion. I accept that as a principle upon which the organization of the war effort of this dominion must take place. To-day we have heard of another instance of gallantry and sacrifice on the part of those who served on the warship that was lost, and greater tests are ahead. The war now enters a period during which stern and ruthless determination must characterize the efforts of all the united nations.
So, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that at a time like this we must have effective administration of national selective service in order to support the men in the forces and to gear up our production in all its phases, agricultural, industrial, mining and forestry. I find it difficult to understand why, after all the declarations that have been made, civilian industries not directly necessary in the war effort still continue to employ many thousands of men and women. I selected a number of these industries indiscriminately with a view to placing the matter before the government, in order to indicate that in this country we have various civilian industries employing more men than they employed before the war began, from which man-power has not been combed. I remember reading an article by

War Appropriation-Labour
Mr. Dexter in April, 1943, in which he dealt with these various industries. The inquiry he then put was, as to why should there be such numbers engaged in civilian industries not directly necessary in the war effort? I now place the various statistics on the record:
Index numbers of employment (1926=100)
Dee. 1,	Dec. 1,	Dec. 1,Industry	1938	1939	1943Furs 	96-5	114-2	125-6Furniture	88-4	91-6	110-2Musical instruments.. Personal services	50-3	56-2	33-8(laundries, etc.) .. .	141-4	142-3	197-6Retail trade	147-8	151-8	181-8Wholesale trade	119-7	125-9	139-4
I might add that the number of employees in the fur industry stood at 2,336 in 1938, 2,765 in 1939, and 3,040 in 1943. And so I can go through the record showing that since 1939 there has been, in civilian industry, a material increase in the number of employees-with one exception, namely, musical instruments- in spite of the fact that within the last year some seven orders have been passed requiring compulsory transfer from non-essential to essential industry.
The man-power situation in general is in a precarious position to-day in this country. This is admitted by Mr. MacNamara himself, in an interview given in the Financial Post of April 29, 1944. It is pointed out there that the situation generally is most serious; 15,000 men a month are required for the armed services, and have been since December of 1943, according to the information contained in "Canada At War."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: For the home army.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Civilian production goods are not being reduced. Canada still goes on with increasing civilian production. I have the figures here which, because of my limited time, I cannot put all on the record. They show a tremendous increase, to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars, in civilian requirements in Canada. The -total sales of all departments of Canadian department stores in 193S was 8280,799,000; in 1939 it was $291,593,000 and in 1940 it was $326,696,000. In 1943 the sales were $417,495,000. In other wards, civilian production is continuing to increase over what it was before the war, and has not been decreased in order to meet the demands of the army and the services.
In base metals, lumbering and agriculture there is a shortage of man-power. There has been a considerable transfer of men from Quebec to Ontario to work in industry. All these factors point to one thing -that the
problem of man-power is the outstanding problem of 1944. It -is the problem upon the solution of which the war effort of this nation will either continue or diminish. It is the problem upon the solution of which price control must depend; for a balance must be secured between production of civilian goods, sufficient partly to meet -the demand, and the production necessary to the war effort. Underproduction of lumber, base metals and coal will lower war production. That is the problem we face, and none is of greater importance at this time.
The minister has pointed out, and properly so, that a great organization has been set up. Many laws have been passed and many regulations have been promulgated. But, Mr. Chairman laws and regulations will not prove effective unless they are effectively enforced. I wish particularly to -refer to the failure on the part of the government to enforce the law to the end that man-power shall be adequate for the armed services as well as for agriculture, transportation and industry in general. The problem, as we all admit, consists in assurance of reinforcements, assurance of food production, and assurance of the necessary supplies for the munitions of war. The Prime Minister enunciated the policy of the government on March 24, 1942, in these words:
Compulsion will -be applied without fear or favour, wherever in the opinion of the government its use will aid in the achievement of a maximum war effort.
That was the promise. To-day we have a record of the performance.
I repeat -that the keystone of unity upon which this country must be built is that of equality -of service. I do not blame the minister for the present condition of affairs; for I do not think he has received the cooperation of the other members of the cabinet -to -the end that there should be equality of service. I pointed oht a year ago that unless the regulations were uniformly applied, antagonism would be built up. I suggested the setting -up of an appeal board to the end that from the Atlantic to the Pacific there should be uniformity of application of the law of selective service.
We come now to a period when the manpower situation is serious. We were given a great many statistics the other day in connection with this matter. But, Mr. Chairman, there is no statistician who can analyse the figures on man-power which have been laid before this parliament and the country. The figures given as of January, 1943, were full and complete. We analysed that statement; so they changed the set-up and detail. During
War Appropriation-Labour

the 1943 session various returns were brought down, all based upon dissimilar hypotheses, all based upon different foundations.

speechtext: And none of them agreeing.

They could not be
expected to agree. In 1944, at this session, the same procedure is followed-one type of return, then another, then a third, but all so arranged that unless one devoted many years to a study of them it would be impossible to analyse the figures.

Is not that men and

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Furthermore, at a time when we are short of men, when men are required, for instance, in the pulpwood industry, and the Department of Labour allowed 3,500 men to go to the United States, and the period during which they may remain in the United States has been extended beyond April 1, 1944.

And is
indefinite.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It has been made indefinite. If ever there was a time when it was necessary to take out pulpwood and to assure the press of this country of its fair and proper share of paper, it is now. Yet, on the one hand, the government admits having a shortage of man-pawer in the woods; so short indeed is that man-power that they have to take in Japanese and prisoners of war. On the other hand they allow 3,500 men to be sent across the line into the United States.
Here, then, is the situation: For 1944, 96,000 men are required for the armed services; 72,000 men are required for industry; men are required in the woods to cut pulpwood, where our production was 200,000,000 feet less than it should have been last year, and yet 3,500 trained men are given permission to leave Canada and cross into the United States to help in the war effort of that nation.
I come to the next question, the administration of the call-up. I want to speak as dispassionately as I can on this subject. The minister has stated that this year the number of delinquents is only some 49,000, and that the position has improved very much as a result of what has been done during the last year. Well, I have the various reports regarding the call-ups under N.R.M.A. before me, and I placed them together in order to see what, the picture is. I have taken the returns which were brought down to the house; I have taken the various issues of "Canada at War"; and they, together with the answers to questions that have been-asked in regard to

War Appropriation-Labour
man-power, are evidence of the practice of mathematical sleight-of-hand in order to secure credit for the government.
"Canada at War'' shows that there is no equal enforcement of the law across Canada. I said that before, and I am not going to go into it in detail again; for no attempt has ever been made by the government to deny it. But I will repeat that in this country to-day there is a spread, with respect to callups and voluntary enlistments, of from 9-8 per cent of the male population between the ages of eighteen and forty-five to 42-7 per cent in the Toronto district, which according to the latest returns has the highest record, followed by Victoria, Halifax and Saint John.
What of the record of enforcement? I shall refer to return 142E, brought down on April 27 in answer to certain questions I asked. I refer also to what the minister said at page 4039 of Hansard of June 23, 1943. As a result I find that in this country a great legion of men between eighteen and forty-five years of age have disappeared without a trace. The minister said that only 49,001 are now unaccounted for, as compared with 67,674 a year ago. But that favourable statement is not borne out by the records. The records on this question cannot be balanced, and in many cases they show a fictional disregard of the actual facts. Take the return I mentioned a moment ago. It shows that the number of men called up was 1,449,417, and that the number who reported was 979,569. That means that 469,848 are unaccounted for, less 71,545, who, according to return 142A, enlisted, on receipt of the order. There is still a balance of some 390,000 missing men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is
the lost army of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And the serious
part of it is that this number is increasing. Last year the explanation given for this tremendous spread was that the machinery was not in operation. The statement given by the minister a year ago showed that 998,475 had been called up and that 608,642 had reported. Last year, as of June 23, 379,833 were unaccounted for. Deducting the numbers of those who must have enlisted, we find that there has been an increase within the past eight months of approximately 60,000 in the number of men unaccounted for.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Four
divisions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Where are the men of this lost legion?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In the bush, like the
government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The figures seem
like an intentional jumble of inconsistency. Where is this army of the vanished-the unfound-the undiscovered? I want the minister to explain that, and not by statements such as he made before, that no doubt some volunteered and got into the army and some went into the merchant marine.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Where are the records to show it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
They say they have their records, and very detailed records, today. All we ask is that they account for approximately 360,000 missing men. A year ago they said that the reason for inequality in the call-up was that in some provinces the. number of fit men was higher than in others. But however good that explanation may have been, the statistics I have given have nothing at all to do with the state of health of the men. The item before us deals with a sum of money to provide for the national selective service programme, one of the functions of which is to make certain that all of Canada's available man-power will be *utilized in the national interest. In this connection I should like to refer to one particular group of men in the city of Winnipeg who have gone back to work. I refer to men over sixty-five years of age who were formerly. employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway company in the Weston shops, who have been given extensions and have gone back to work in order to assist in all-out production. Naturally among men of that advanced age only those physically able to return to work are so employed, which focuses attention on the fact that many other men of the same age and *circumstances have not been able to accept

extensions for further employment, and find themselves in a difficult position because of the fact that in many cases no pension is available to them. This raises a question of labour relations which I should like to draw as forcibly as I can to the attention of the minister and the government in the hope that.it may be given serious consideration.
As from January 1,1937, the Canadian Pacific Railway company instituted a new pension scheme for its employees on a contributory basis, as distinct from the non-contributory plan which had been in existence for many years. Into that new plan was written a provision which has created a serious problem for many men, the effects of which are now being felt. I refer to section 8(a) of the rules of that pension plan, which reads in part as follows:
Only those employees of the company shall be eligible for pension whose names are entered on its staff records, whose last entry into its service has or shall have occurred before attaining the age of forty years-
When this new plan was set up in 1937 the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway company, at the Weston shops and elsewhere in Winnipeg, realized what it would mean a few years hence and, as I say, the effects of this plan now are being felt very keenly by hundreds of employees. To go for a moment into the background of this situation, I would remind the minister that in 1919 a serious strike occurred in the city of Winnipeg, in which many thousands of men participated. Of those who went out during the course of that strike, four thousand were employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When the railway company instituted this new pension plan it ruled that employees who had been out of work during the course of that strike should be regarded as having terminated their employment. In other words, no matter for how many years prior to 1919 these men might have worked for the company, their employment was dated as of the date of their return in that year. When this new plan was first studied by the men affected it was found that there were still in the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Winnipeg, in 1937, 2,500 men whose employment had been interrupted during the strike of 1919. Of these some 2,100, when they returned to work in 1919, were still under the age of forty; in other words it was their right, when the new plan came into effect in 1937, to become participants in that plan since they were under the age limit prescribed when they returned to work. However, many of these 2,100 men had put in quite a number of years of sendee prior to 1919, so that even in their case the benefits of those years of service

War Appropriation-Labour
have been lost under the new pension plan. The other four hundred who were still in the employ of the company in 1937 were men who had been over forty years of age when they returned to work in 1919, so when the new plan came into effect they were denied the right to enter into it or participate in any pension scheme whatsoever. Hon. members will recognize at once that as a result many men who have given twenty, thirty or forty years of their lives in the service of the company in Winnipeg, upon retirement at the age of sixty-five are not eligible to receive pensions from the company.
As hon. gentlemen will expect, this matter was carefully considered by the unions affected, and in due course in 1937 they took it up with their general chairmen. Later a subcommittee of these general chairmen took the matter up with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the late Sir Edward Beatty. The matter was under consideration from, roughly, December, 1937, until well into 1939. The last conference between the subcommittee of the general chairmen and the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company took place on July 3, 1939. On October 18 of that year the subcommittee reported on their efforts to the unions affected, and I should like to quote briefly from the report given at that time. This is from the report of the subcommittee of the general chairmen back to1 the unions affected:
After going very carefully into tile matter at issue it was stated by Mr. Coleman that, apart altogether from the fact that the strikes in question were in violation of the law of the land, viz., the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and were further unauthorized by the organizations now making a plea on behalf of these men-many of whom had gone on strike after the recognized representatives of the unions had . advised against such action

the company was now being asked to find more than $1,250,000 in addition to the amount already required to meet normal expenditures for pension purposes. He made it very clear that the earnings of the company made such a task quite impossible, and regretted very much that, in such circumstances, he had to deny the request of the committee.
Further in this same report I find this:
We have kept in close touch with this matter over a considerable period of time, always encouraged by the hope that sufficient improvement might take place in the financial condition of the company as to enable us to realize a firm conviction which we have always held that, in such improved conditions at least, some relief might be forthcoming.
Later I find the general chairmen saying this:
We are still of the unanimous view that, had the financial conditions of the company been different, we would have made progress.
I have read those quotations to emphasize what appeared to be the view of the committee which met the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, namely, that the chief obstacle so far as the company was concerned was the expense involved in meeting the request of the men. It will be noted that the official concerned, Mr. Coleman, stated there were two matters involved, first, that the strike in 1919 had

So far as I know this
matter has not been raised before and I do not see how the suggestion of repetition is involved. It seems to me I should be permitted to continue, because this is a matter of great concern. I believe I should be allowed to proceed under the general heading of labour relations in time of war.

I should like to emphasize that Mr. Coleman's reply to these men was twofold; first, that in his view the strike was illegal, and second, that from the standpoint of the company the money could not be found to finance the pensions these men were requesting. In reply to the argument that the strike was illegal I would point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is the only large employer in Winnipeg which, so far as a programme of pensions is concerned, still takes cognizance of the 1919 strike. The Canadian National Railways were in the picture at the time. Later on they likewise instituted a new pension scheme, dating I believe from January 1, 1935; but no discrimination is levelled against any employees of that company who were out in 1919, as has happened in the case of the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The same holds true with respect to the dominion government. It took back its postal employees and other government employees in Winnipeg, and did not cut into their pension rights at all because of the events of that year. The same is true of the Manitoba provincial government, and of the city of Winnipeg, having special reference to the police of that city who were out during the course of the strike. It seems to me the commendable attitude all these other large employers have taken, including the dominion government itself, both as a government and through its connection with the Canadian National Railways, is the best answer to that argument.
The suggestion that the strike was illegal implies that the company feel that they lost money as a result thereof. Actually that is not so. There had been built up, through the fact that these men would have qualified for a pension on a non-contributory basis, had they stayed on, an equity which in fact was theirs. The company says it would cost them $1,200,000 to pay that equity to these men. It is admitting that it has made $1,200,000 out of the strike whereas, as I have already pointed out, other large employers have not taken advantage of their men in that way.
Answering the argument that the company cannot afford to pay these pensions, first of all I emphasize the fact that these men had an equity which belonged to them in the period prior to 1919. In connection with every -wage negotiation which took place during that period, when the men were seeking higher wages, the company always pointed to the non-contributory pension plan as a factor which should be taken into consideration. In other words it assumed there was an equity under the former plan which belonged to the men.
I would point out, too, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have had a great deal given to them by way of land grants, grants of money and tax exemptions right across this country, and that they have a responsibility not only to individual employees, such as those on behalf of whom I speak, but to the community as a whole.
I well remember during the depression years of the thirties, because I was living in Weston at the time in the home of an employee of the company, how these men agreed to a reduction in the number of their working days to as few as ten a moltth in order that there might be a minimum of actual lay-offs in the Weston shops. I would point out that the men by accepting this course and thus avoiding widespread lay-offs saved money for the taxpayers of the country and also saved the Canadian Pacific Railway Company from demands that would undoubtedly have been made upon it to provide funds to 'keep these men going had they been laid off.
There is one other point that should be emphasized when the company is insisting that it cannot pay these pensions, and that is to be found in the financial reports which the company has been making in the last two or three years. I find that the net railway earnings of the company in 1941, for example, were $45,957,536; in 1942, the net railway earnings were $48,187,689, and in 1943, $49,211,567. After making certain deductions and adjustments which appear in the figures listed in the company's own reports which I have before me, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was still able in 1943 to add $37,939,936 to its profit and loss account, with the result that at the end of 1943 the credit balance in its profit and loss account was $239,190,419. I suggest that in the face of those figures the argument that the company cannot afford to pay the pensions which belong to these men is utterly ridiculous.
I have before me the details of a number of these cases. I shall not take time to go into them but I should like a few minutes to tell the story of one employee of the company, the file on whose case I have in my hand.
This employee entered the service of the company in 1912 and was with the company until 1942, a total of thirty years. In 1923 he had an accident while at work and lost a leg. In 1942, when he was 64 years and 3 months of age, his health became so poor that it was impossible for him to continue at work, and so the company wrote him a nice letter giving him leave of absence because of his illness, without pay. Nine months later he received another letter telling

War Appropriation-Labour
him that now he was sixty-five years of age he would be retired. But of course there was no pension because this employee was out of the service for a time in 1919.
When this employee wrote to the company and asked for consideration in view of his distress and his need, the reply that was sent to him, and which I have before me, said that the company were sorry but that nothing could be done under the rules as they stood, and the company were also very sorry that the man's health was such that he could not avail himself of an extension and go back to work, and keep himself alive in that way. . Hon. members will see the position in which that man was put. He gave thirty years of his life; he gave a leg; he gave his health to the company, and all the company had to say in return was: We are sorry your health does not permit you to carry on and work beyond the age of sixty-five and thus keep yourself alive. And that at a time when the company is making the profits which I have already indicated.
These men, as I have already said, have taken this matter up repeatedly through their unions and through the chairmen of their organizations, and they have also endeavoured to take the matter up as individuals with the officials of the company. A short while ago, when Mr. Coleman was passing through Winnipeg, one of these men wrote him a personal letter stating the position in which he found himself and stating that others were in the same circumstances. He wrote this, in part, to Mr. Coleman:
While we are aware of the failure of our general chairmen on this question, we think that the case might be placed in a more appealing way by some of the men affected. Hoping, sir, that you will pardon our presumption and grant us this privilege. . . .
In reply to this letter from an individual, Mr. Coleman under date of July 3, 1942, said in part:
I was in charge of western lines at the time [DOT] of the 1919 strike and am familiar with all the circumstances, and conducted the negotiations with the labour representatives. I have never felt that there was any injustice involved in the decisions then made.
I emphasize to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that the decisions made by the Canadian Pacific were wholly at variance with the decisions made by the Canadian National, the dominion government, the provincial government and the city of Winnipeg. I am satisfied that in Winnipeg to-day, despite the feelings of the past about the 1919 strike, all would agree that this matter should be
reconsidered and that these men should be given their pensions. Mr. Coleman went on to say:
There would, therefore, be no advantage in having a discussion with me. If there are any special circumstances surrounding your case, which may have been overlooked, I suggest that you communicate with Mr. Mather.
Regretting that I am unable to write you in more encouraging terms, I remain,
Yours very truly,
D. C. Coleman,
. President.
All of this, as matters now stand, apparently seems to be under the complete control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The unions and their general chairmen have done their best in the matter, but the company has turned them down. I suggest that the argument that the company could not finance the pensions for these men, even if it had any merit years ago when it was made to the general chairmen, certainly has no validity to-day.
In addition to these efforts by the general chairmen, the individuals themselves have made efforts such as those to which I have just referred, but without avail.
We are forced back to the terms of the Railway Act, by which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and other railways apparently were given power to set up their own pension schemes without having to submit them to review by the federal government. The appropriate section of the Railway Act is section 122, which reads in part as follows:
The directors may make by-laws or pass resolutions, from time to time, not inconsistent with law, for
(c) the retirement of such of said officers and servants, on such terms as to an annual allowance or otherwise, as in each case the directors, in the interest of the company's service, and under the circumstances, consider just and reasonable.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if it is necessary for the government to submit an amendment to the Railway Act in order to take care of this matter, the government should give consideration to such a course. If, on the other hand, it can be taken care of as a matter of labour relations where improvement is necessary for the war effort, I hope that the Minister of Labour will look into the matter. The section of the Railway Act which I have just quoted seems to have given the entire say over to the company. In other words, the employees concerned, who give their health and their lives in the manner I have indicated have no redress through their government, through the people whom they democratically elect to represent them.
War Appropriation-Labour

I would urge that the government take this matter under consideration in an effort to see whether something cannot be done for these men. Whatever the views may have been about the 1919 strike; whatever ideas with respect to pensions and social legislation may have prevailed in those days, we are living now in a different era, when the country as a whole feels that working men are entitled to a proper share of the wealth they produce, and entitled in their old age to decent pension. I submit that these men have been dealt with most unjustly, that they have been discriminated against as compared with employees of the other large organizations to which I have referred, and I hope that this matter will be given consideration by the minister, or by the government.

speechtext:
I have considerable
familiarity with the facts dealt with by the last speaker. I know that the problem concerning the Canadian Pacific railway's fund is not, strictly and technically a government matter. Prior to the time that it changed its superannuation plan the Canadian Pacific had one which was non-contributory. It was not a bad scheme, when one considers that no direct contribution by the employees was required. Later the Canadian Pacific changed over to a plan which is quite similar to that of the Canadian National; at least there are many points of similarity. This change occurred not very many years ago. I do not think that at the time they were drawing up the by-laws for the new plan they had in mind particularly the 2,500 employees-if 2,500 is the right figure, in the Weston area who had been on strike in the big general strike of 1919. However, the result was that most of these men, or at any rate a large number of them, could not acquire pension rights, because of the break in their service in 1919. As I have said, I realize that it is not strictly a government matter, but I know the Department of Labour took a hand in it at some times in the past and endeavoured to effect changes beneficial to the men. While I do not think it is feasible to pass a law to coerce the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I would urge that the department be astute to try to discover some way of influencing the Canadian Pacific.
I may tell the committee a story with reference to this sort of thing, the facts respecting which I know personally, because of the source from which they come. There was a strike on the Grand Trunk railway back in 1907 or 1908. The men lost that strike. When it wras coming to am endi, the

then deputy minister of labour, the present Prime Minister of this country, made a bargain with Mr. Hays, who wTas the president of that railway, that, despite the men having lost, he would restore them to work as fast as opportunity offered. Notwithstanding everything that the then deputy minister, Mr. King, could do, Mr. Hays welshed on his bargain and did not take the men back to work, and they were scattered all over Canada working for other railways. I myself met many of them in the ten or fifteen years of railroad work that I did. All of them lost their jobs in spite of what was done by [DOT] the man who later became the Prime Minister of this country.
The sequel to that story is as follows. In 1911 the president of that railway was looking for money from the Canadian government, The then deputy minister of labour had become a minister of the crown, and he said to Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time, "Unless Hays acts differently from what he has done in the past-and he is not entitled to this consideration-I would not grant it to him." As a matter of fact the minister took the position that he would resign from the cabinet if Hays, without keeping his undertaking, got consideration to which he was not legally entitled. Sir Wilfrid Laurier delivered an ultimatum to the president of the railway, and parliament was dissolved in 1911 without his obtaining the government aid which he sought. Mr. King, the minister at that time, was defeated in that election. The next time he had to deal with the problem was after he became Prime Minister of this country, when Sir Henry Thornton was being appointed. At that time conversations were held with Thornton, and the Prime Minister, as Mr. King then was, after telling him the whole story, said, "I do not make it a condition of your appointment that these men will even yet get such measure of justice as can be given them, but I do make it a condition of the appointment that you will personally look into it". It was not more than six or seven months later that every one of the sixteen hundred men who had behn discriminated against in 1907 or 190S had been hunted up, and eveiy one of them received whatever compensation could be given in lieu of those that had been taken away. In many cases moneys were paid to their estates. I know these facts to be as I have stated them, and if any minister of the crown is not familiar with the circumstances his best source of information is his own Prime Minister. This measure of justice was effected in this manner by the present

War Appropriation-Labour
Prime Minister. Incidentally, it is altogether too bad that the story is not better known.
I do not know what the Department of Labour can do in a case of this kind, but I submit that it should concern itself to find a way to help these C.P.R. men. I know the minister and his department would desire to do anything that is possible. I do not make any specific recommendation about changing the law; indeed, I do not think a specific recommendation at this moment would be worth while, because it might turn out not to be feasible. But the time may come when the Minister of Labour can find 'a way of helping.
I wish to add just a few further words. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken did, it is true, point out that the pension law of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is out of line with that of the Canadian National Railways. I think it might have been a little more generous on his part had he drawn attention in a very special way to that fact. It was glossed over; it was mentioned but not stressed to any degree. The grievance was brought out into the open and stirred around a good deal, but praise was not given in the generous manner which might have been expected to the Canadian National Railways as an instrument of this government for the fair sort of pension scheme which it has. I suggest to the committee not to overlook, when a grievance is being told, the fact that this government and the instrument of this government have acted in an eminently fair way and have instituted what is probably the best pension scheme on the north American continent. This government has done not merely that which is right but that which is indeed generous, and I think it is no more than fair, when dealing with the subject, to draw attention to it.
There is only one other part of to-day's debate to which I wish to make reference. My comments arise from the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). He was endeavouring to make something out of what he called an unemployment problem, calling attention to the fact that there had been certain payments made from the unemployment insurance fund and trying from that to show that we have a real unemployment problem in this country. The fact of the matter is that when you have unemployment insurance you are bound to have a statistic on unemployment. There has never been a year in any country which had unemployment insurance, no matter how prosperous that country was, when they did not have what some might choose to call an unemployment problem; but the right expression
to use is an unemployment statistic, because when you have unemployment insurance, obviously every person who has paid a premium comes to get his benefit.
In substantiation of what I have said, 1 wish to call attention to this fact. In the two countries whose reports up to the end of last year are at present before us, unemployment insurance benefits have regularly been paid. I refer to Great Britain and New Zealand. The latest reports from Australia are not here, but I am confident that you will find a statistic from Australia. That country, right down into the middle of the war, has been paying unemployment insurance benefits from day to day.

4 Mr. WHITE: I wish to speak briefly on the man-power question, which I think the Minister of National Defence will agree comes under this item. I shall make another one. I do not think the minister could read my shorthand. If the minister would give us a statement setting out these different items as a certain date, it would get over the somewhat confused picture that has been presented to us by the various returns filed in the house.
Apparently the question of man-power is to be an acute one this year, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I know that at least in military district No. 3, which includes the city of Ottawa, there is a very great shortage of man-power. During the past month many young men who had obtained exemptions on account of living and working on farms have received notices, when applying for further extension, that they are to report to district depot No. 3 at Kingston, where they are to be reexamined and reclassified. That may be because of some change in the regulations, or it may be the usual routine procedure. But I do know in the past once a man who has been called for military service has satisfied the divisional registrar that he is a genuine farmer and is actively engaged in agricultural production he is granted a postponement, which is automatically renewed, or he is granted a postponement which reads: "Until further notice." If there is to be some change in this procedure, and if any of those men who are on farms are to be called and taken into the army, I think the minister should tell the committee.
Only to-day I received a letter from Kingston in regard to an extension I wrote about for a cheesemaker who is in charge of a cheese factory in the county of Hastings producing well over 200,000 pounds of cheese a year. His postponement runs out on June 1. The letter was to the effect that he would have to report at Kingston on June 1, when the exemption runs out. If there is to be any change I would point out to the minister that it is unfortunate to call these men off the farms at this particular time of the year, because in the district where I live mixed farming is carried on. The farmers there, in response to requests from the government, have increased the number of stock they carry on the farms; they
War Appropriation-Labour

have brought into cultivation quite a large amount of new ground. If those farmers are now to be deprived of those men who have received exemptions they will be left in a very unsatisfactory position.
I would refer the minister to a statement which appeared in a Belleville newspaper last week. This statement was given by Mr. H. H. Reed, manager of the local branch of the national selective service division at Belleville. The statement reads as follows:
Wages as high as $75 and $80 per month are being offered by the occasional Hastings county farmer for experienced farm help for the coming season, it was stated here to-day by H. H. Reed, *manager, local branch of the national selective service. Demand for farm help is quite steady with the office at present having thirty-six unfilled applications.
That figure may not appear very high to some of the farmer members from the west, but it is in eastern Ontario. As I said a moment ago, I hope that the minister will tell the committee if there is to be any change, or whether this is just the routine procedure and that those men who now have farm postponements will receive a further extension.
I agree with what was said by the minister at the close of his remarks, that the needs of the armed forces must come first, put the armed forces first and agriculture second. At the same time, however, the minister is a member of this government and must realize that the responsibility for securing men for the armed forces and for agriculture rests upon his shoulders and those of the other members of the cabinet. The minister presented a long report, but I would point out that as yet his department has not put into effect in Canada a real policy of selective service under which everyone in this country will be put in the place he is best suited to fill; nor has he yet put into operation a policy under which all men eligible for military service may be sent to any part of the world. How can the minister be consistent when he refers to the shortage of man-power that exists to-day, while at the same time he supports a policy under which, according to figures supplied by the government, there remains in this country a home defence army of from
75,000	to 100,000 men, who under present regulations cannot be sent out of the country? As was so well pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, if we are to have unity in this country there must be equality of service and sacrifice. One has only to examine the various reports and returns published in "Canada at War" to see the unfair quotas filled by voluntary enlistment in the various provinces. I have said before in this house, and I repeat, that I could never understand

why one province should be expected to contribute a much larger number of men to the armed forces than any other province.

Yes, in relation to population. I say the policy of the government in obtaining men for the armed forces is one of political expediency; and I do not understand how they can expect to run a political war and at the same time create national unity. We all remember the great fuss that took place in this house at the time of the plebiscite. I was a member of the committee which revised the rules in that connection; the matter was so urgent that the committee was required to complete its work in two days. They were obliged to sit in the morning, the afternoon and until late at night in order that the bill might be brought into the house and rushed through. Well, we had the plebiscite; eight provinces voted "yes" and one province voted "no", but the conditions which existed before the plebiscite was taken exist to-day, and the regulations are exactly the same. The government continues its policy of attempting to induce men in the home defence army to go active. As I have said before, the responsibility for obtaining these men rests upon the shoulders of the government; it is a responsibility which cannot be delegated to any officers of the army. It is most humiliating for any officer, no matter what his rank may be, to have to appeal to men in the home defence army to go active. During the course of his remarks on Thursday last, as reported at page 2383 of Hansard, the minister said:
It seems to me that the army is not only entitled to see to it, ibut it is the duty of the army to see to it, that the needs of the volunteer army are put before the people of Canada in exactly the same way.
I think the minister is wrong in that statement, because it is his department and the government who decide what are to be the needs of the army and how these men are to be obtained. It would be very nice for the minister and his department to pass the responsibility for securing recruits for the active army over to the officers. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it all results from the failure of the government to adopt a policy under which men eligible for military service could be sent outside Canada. During the course of his remarks on the same occasion, at the same page, the minister went on to say:
. .	. I deprecate more than I can say the
attempt which has been made to disparage recruiting activities in Canada.

War Appropriation-Labour
The minister did not refer to any particular person or body of people, but I would draw to his attention the motion that was adopted in the Quebec legislature only last week. By a vote of some fifty-four to four the house approved a motion stating that they were opposed to sending any conscripted men overseas. The minister belongs to' the same political party that is in power in Quebec, but as yet I have not heard any hon. member of this house repudiate or condemn the motion in question. Does the minister think a motion of this kind, on the very eve of the invasion, is in the interests of national unity, that it is in the interests of recruiting or that it will help the troops overseas? Are they going to feel that the citizens of Canada are behind them when they read of such a motion being passed by the Quebec house? Several members of the cabinet come from Quebec. If they do not approve that motion I think it is their duty and responsibility to say so in this house and to repudiate the motion that was adopted by such a huge majority.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I said I deprecated the efforts being made by some people to discourage recruiting activities. The hon. member is talking about some motion passed by a provincial legislature which opposed the sending of conscripted men overseas. Those are two different things. I say that my hon friend is not only absolutely unjustified in his remarks but that he is doing something which is harmful to Canada's war effort when he suggests that it is humiliating to request officers to ask men to enlist, or to endeavour to see that they do enlist. I say that part of the job we have to do is to get men. My hon. friend has not suggested that there is anything objectionable when we are asked by the national war finance committee to bring back officers and men from overseas to ask me and him and all other hon. members of this house as well as the public in general to subscribe their money for the purpose of supporting those men. That is perfectly all right, but when officers of the army ask men to enlist, that is humiliating. I say that my hon. friend is making a statement derogatory to the war effort and absolutely unjustified, and one which comes from just the sort of attitude I mentioned the other day, namely, not so much a desire to see men come into the army but rather a desire to see that men come into the army through conscription.

I can only say to the minister I repeat that it is humiliating for any officer, no matter what his rank may be, to have to plead with men whom he is supposed to lead, 100-158
to enlist in the active army. Those men are already in the home defence army, and it is the duty of the minister and the government to get them into the army. The minister and the government are the ones to set the policy. It is not up to the officers, and they have no authority-I will not say they have no authority, but the government is not right in trying to shove off on to the shoulders of officers the responsibility of obtaining men for service overseas.	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What does my hon. friend think this house has been voting money for, for recruiting officers and recruiting organizations, for the last two or three years? Has my hon. friend any objection to that? Does my hon. friend think the vote is wrong? We have had recruiting staffs in every part of the country-and so has the navy, and so has the air force. Does my hon. friend suggest that those procedures are wrong on the part of the officers of the navy or the air force? These staffs are employed for that very purpose; these officers are employed for that very purpose. Is there any humiliation in working in that particular job? The air member for personnel in the air force and the officer dealing with personnel in the navy, have as part of their responsibilities the getting of men to enlist in the navy and the air force. The adjutant-general in the army has the same job. Does my hon. friend suggest that that is a humiliating activity?

I say again it is a humiliating activity-and the minister is not cross-examining me. While the minister speaks that way about obtaining recruits for the army I should like to refer him to the record of a recent meeting of the Ontario command of the legion. I am sure that no one will even suggest that members of the legion would do anything in the slightest degree to hinder or to harm the welfare of the armed forces of Canada. This was the motion passed at a recent meeting in Toronto of the Ontario command:
This convention reaffirms the legion's mandate of 1941-"The legion's call for total war," and strongly asks the federal government for its immediate implementation in the matter of calling men for service anywhere.
The editorial continues:
The legion does not believe in bludgeoning the draftees on to active service. They, the men who fought in the last war, refuse to be part of the campaign of shaming, of coercing men to go active. They realize that the fair way, the honest way, is for the government to pass the order in council which would send anywhere those who are in the home defence army. And in that course the legion is in keeping with the view of the majority of Canadians who voted "yes" in the plebiscite.

War Appropriation-Labour

At the game meeting Mr. Alex Walker, dominion president of the Canadian legion, is reported in the press as speaking as follows:
I don't think the government should have officers going around and telling men to do their duty. Why couldn't the government put into power the authority it has and tell these men (in the home defence army) they are going wherever required? No one need fear the Canadian Legion. Our feet are on the ground, and in whatever we do we think first of Canada and then of ourselves. If more people would think of the country first and then of their political fences, it would be a better Canada to-day.
And the legion speaks not only for nearly all members of the armed forces of the last war, but also for a very large number of other citizens in Canada.

speechtext: If my hon. friend's attitude is correct, then what should be done is to take off the road all mobile recruiting units of the whole three services, and simply wait for the men to volunteer. That was not done in the last war, and it has not been done in this war so far in any of the three services. I do not propose that it shall be done, so far as the army is concerned, and I believe my colleagues feel the same way about the navy and the air force.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of care the other day as the Minister of Labour made his statement to the committee, and I have since had an opportunity of reading his statement. I realize, as I have said in the past, that he has a tremendous job on his hands. There are many things that go to magnify the troubles of the Department of Labour. As I listened to the minister and as I have watched his work over the years, he seems to me a very conscientious, sort of fellow who is working under great difficulty. He has to have two objectives always before him. He has to administer national selective service so as to ensure that there will be a sufficient supply of labour on the farms and in industry, and at the same time he has some responsibility for seeing that a sufficient number of men are left available to enter the home defence forces. So that he is really working at cross-purposes. Not only is he compelled to satisfy the Department of Labour and ensure that the demands of labour for better wages and better working conditions are met, but he has also to satisfy the three branches of the Department of National Defence, and has to satisfy also the Department of Finance. All this tends to magnify the difficulties of the position in which the minister finds himself. All these different aspects of his work have to dove-tail into one another as well as they can, and in some respects the minister is doing a very well worth-while job.
One notable feature of the minister's statement to the committee the other day was the educational training that is being given to civilians in war industry and to those who are being rehabilitated. That is commendable, but in that connection it must be borne in mind, and I am sure that the people of Canada will have this in mind, that there is not much use in training people for different jobs, especially civilians and those engaged in the war industries, if there are to be no jobs for them after the war. One of the big things which this country has to do after winning the war, which I think we all agree is our first objective, is 100-1581
to see that there will be jobs for our men after they return home, and jobs that will be remunerative-not the kind of job that was going during the depression when a man could hardly make a living for himself and family. The returned man will expect a great deal more than that after this war, and rightly so. I could hardly conceive of the men being satisfied if, after they got home, they found the same conditions that prevailed during the depression years. Yet I have noticed a great deal of political propaganda that is going out all over the country and to the armed forces, some of it broadcast over the air, all to the effect that great preparations are being made in this country for the post-war period. I just do not believe that. Some measures are being taken, but very few. Actually we are not doing a great deal to ensure that when our men return from overseas they will find Canada a really well worth-while country.
There has been a great deal of talk here this afternoon about the war effort and the necessity for getting recruits. But if we are in a position to assure our people that this Canada of ours is to be a really well worthwhile place after this war is won, we shall not have so much difficulty in getting recruits. Now you cannot ensure that, merely by putting out a lot of propaganda. To-day I received a bunch of pamphlets from the Liberal organization. They were addressed to J. A. Johnston but they came to me and I opened them by mistake. These pamphlets were on post-war reconstruction-what is to be done for the soldiers after the war. I could not see that there was a great deal in the pamphlets that was true, as I glanced over them, because really we have not done a great deal. We have a social security measure before us, but it is a long way from being put into effect, and I doubt whether the whole of it will ever be put into effect, though parts of it may be.
