speechtext: Who sent the pamphlets?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Liberal organization. I have not that in mind alone. A great many pamphlets have been got out by the government themselves and sent to members of the active forces, giving the idea that great preparations are being made in Canada for the post-war period. Those boys are going to be badly mistaken if when they come back they find that actually very little has been done to prepare for the post-war period. That is one of the difficulties in which the Minister of Labour finds himself.
The minister in his statement to the committee the other day referred to certain industries in Canada, and I was particularly
War Appropriation-Labour

interested in what he said about the coal industry, because there is a coal industry in my part of the country. I know very well that the minister might say that that is a purely local question, that the conditions there apply in only one area of Canada. But that would not be true. 'It is true that in Nova Scotia there are not the same difficulties in coal mining that there are in Alberta. But conditions in Alberta are not just a temporary thing. They demand attention and have done so for a long time, and they call for planning to carry us over a crisis. It is summertime now and perhaps our coal requirements do not seem so pressing at the moment, but winter will come again, and as the minister stated in his speech some weeks ago, now is the time to start planning. But no planning with regard to the coal industry has been done apart from the announcement that a royal commission is to be set up to investigate conditions in the coal industry, with a view, I suppose, to creating a national fuel policy. We have needed a national fuel policy for a number of years now. I have advocated such a policy ever since I came into this house in 1935. That is a long time, and I am not very hopeful that the royal commission which is to be set up will have any far-reaching effects in the establishment of a permanent fuel policy for Canada. Why? Because we have had these things in the past, and up to the present no action has been taken as a result.
Speaking on Friday last, the minister said, as reported in Hansard at page 2438:
The situation of the coal mining industry was declared to be a national emergency in May, 1943. . . .
It was a national emergency at that time. We remember what a desperate need there was in all parts of Canada for coal, and drastic measures were taken at that time to overcome the emergency. In my opinion we are drifting right now to the same position we were in last winter. We are depleting the mines of their help; the miners are being scattered again here and there, and it would not surprise me if we found ourselves in a much worse position than before. It will be recalled that on the last occasion we were able to alleviate the shortage by having soldier miners sent back to the mines. We may not be able to repeat that operation this coming winter because a great number of these men may have gone overseas. We cannot foretell conditions as regards the defence of this country and whether we shall be able to send soldier miners from the home defence army for occupation in the mines if an emergency should arise. Certainly we shall not be in any better
TMr. C. E. Johnston.]
position this coming winter to obtain the services of miners who are seasonally occupied in agriculture. It follows that by every indication the condition will be worse this coming winter than it was last winter.
The minister went on to say:
Last May, order in council P.C. 4092 was [DOT]passed, and directed that men with coal-mining experience then engaged in other industry, and who were physically fit, should 'be returned to the mines.
From the point of view of emergency that policy was all right, and it did assist in overcoming the emergency. I have never criticized the principle of selective service; in fact, I thought it was the proper thing as soon as the war began, and our group was the first in the house to advocate it. But the administration in many of the local areas was extremely faulty, as I have pointed out to the minister on other occasions.
One instance which I recall, and which I do not think I have brought to his attention before, was drawn to my attention by the words he used which I have just quoted, "who were physically fit". Five men were sent from Ontario to the Drumheller area by national selective service. It may be a regulation, in accordance with the minister's reference to men "who were physically fit", that there should be a medical examination by competent authority to ascertain that they are physically fit; but the five men sent from Ontario, who were supposed to be miners, were too old to do the job, and were proved by medical inspection in Drumheller to be physically unfit for it. They could not stand the work, and after working two or three shifts they were compelled to quit their jobs. This was an unfortunate occurrence not only from the point of view of the cost to which the state was put in sending these men three thousand miles or more and withdrawing them from the armed forces, but because of the inconvenience and disturbance to which the mining company itself was put. All five men returned, and it is definitely known that the return fares of three of them had to be paid. The unnecessary expense was incurred of transferring these five men from Ontario to Drumheller, taking up valuable space on the trains, and transporting them back again. Altogether eight men were sent. Three others who came from Camp Borden had had no experience in coal mining, though they had had hard rock mining experience in Ontario. The minister says that they were physically fit. Probably they should have been, but definitely they were not. There has been no effort to overcome such situations as that.

War Appropriation-Labour
Matters have now gone to the other extreme, and in both Calgary and Edmonton districts coal mines are having to shut down. When last I spoke on this question, a few weeks ago, having reference in particular to the closing of the * mines at Edmonton, I was assured by the minister that national selective service was operating so wonderfully that, should the mines close down, these men would immediately be taken care of; in fact the minister thought I was unduly pessimistic about that situation. As the facts have developed, it does not seem that I was, because, I am informed, the mines did close down and some of these men are not yet reemployed and are still receiving unemployment insurance. That is not a satisfactory condition when we are supposed to be having an all-out war effort in which everyone is taking his place.
In the Drumheller area the same situation prevails, possibly to a greater extent. I am informed by a letter recently received that in that mining area a great deal of trouble is occurring with national selective service in the payment of men who are receiving unemployment insurance. Since the mines closed, large numbers of men have been forced to apply for unemployment insurance, but have had difficulty in getting their pay. Sometimes it is delayed two or three weeks, or even longer, and the situation is coming to a point where the miners are about ready to take drastic action unless something is done. These conditions, which are directly related to selective service and unemployment insurance, require considerable attention by the minister.
There is one other item to which I wish to refer, because I think it too touches on this problem of national selective service. There has been some talk this afternoon about the defence army, and since this comes under the man-power policy, I would refer to a few remarks made by the minister himself. When he was speaking the other day he had this to say, as reported at page 2430 of Hansard, with reference to the man-power policy:
In my opinion the true yardstick of a successful man-power policy is the degree to which the armed forces are mobilized for the job of fighting, and the material resources organized for maximum output of munitions, food and all the other things necessary.
I will agree with him in that statement, that the true yardstick is the result of policy. I wonder how true that has proved to be? Let us see what he said further on, because under the minister's department comes the duty of getting men for the defence army.
He has to supply them and, after they are in there, they are out of his department. We have been given so many pictures of our mobilization effort that it is exceedingly difficult to know just where we stand, but as reported at page 2445 of Hansard the minister said, in the same speech:
We are now finding it more difficult to fill the army requisitions. As the war progresses, it is evident that we will soon have to rely largely upon those at present deferred and the young men coming of age.
I said at the opening of my remarks that the minister was between two fires: he had to supply men for the defence plants, civilian occupations, and also get men for the home defence army. He goes on to say:
The proportion of fit men in the higher age classes is becoming increasingly smaller. This entails a greater effort for smaller returns.
There is another point I would like to mention. Recently my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (army), made the statement in the house that he would require 60,000 men in the year commencing the first of April. In further correspondence with me, he has stressed the absolute necessity of obtaining these men, particularly bearing in mind the requirements of operations which are in. prospect.
I would call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that there is a great deal of concern about the man-power problem in the arm3r in the very near future. Here we have a statement about the absolute necessity of obtaining these men, particularly bearing in mind the requirements of operations in prospect. There cannot be any fooling about that. The Minister of National Defence has pointed out to the Minister of Labour the great danger that lies ahead and the great need for sufficient recruits for the army. He is taking great care to point that out. I quote further:
In the last six months, September 1943 to February 1944, there actually have been more than 5,000 men per month who were enlisted' and enrolled in the army alone. However, the monthly average has been decreasing, and at times enlistments and enrolments have fallen below the numbers required by the army. For this reason I think it is only fair to state in the house that further postponements in industry generally will have to ibe curtailed. This policy should not adversely affect industry; for, as I have already stated, Its maximum demand has been passed. I mention this in order that all members will realize that the retention of young men of military age and fitness in industry can only be justified under very exceptional circumstances.
That brings me to the question which has been partly discussed this afternoon, of getting men from the farms and from industry to meet this shortage of man-power in the army. When the Minister of National Defence was speaking I was surprised at some of the things lie had to say with regard to the method of
War Appropriation-Labour

getting these men, and I doubt very much whether the Minister of Labour agrees with the present policy of obtaining men for the armed forces. He may, though I am inclined to think he does not. The duty of the Minister of Labour is to see wherever possible that men are made available for the defence army. I recall apearing before the board in Edmonton a couple of years ago when I was endeavouring to get some farm lads postponed. As a matter of fact, I got the postponements because the board was very reasonable and saw the necessity. But this was the situation as they put it up to me: Here we have received an order from Ottawa directing us in this district to obtain 25,000 young men; we are not told where to get them but we must go and get them. The chairman of the board said to me, "Where would you get them? You are a westerner and you know that we have got nearly all the boys in the towns. Where shall we get these 25,000? Yet we have received an order from Ottawa to get them." Obviously there was only one place where they could be got, namely, out of industry or from the farms The minister's problem, therefore, is becoming more and more magnified as the situation to which he refers becomes more acute. I do not know where he will get men, but I am opposed to the method that is used now. I am wholly against the method used to obtain these men from the draft army into the active army, and I am amazed at the attitude taken by the two old line parties in this house over this question.

speechtext: We never had political ambitions. The member for York-Sunbury says we never had political ambitions and I am glad he recognizes that. I am sorry that I cannot say the same for his party. When the plebiscite was on, the same thing happened. It was a political issue. There again we stood out differently from all the others. But when you advocate a policy such as that you cannot expect to have any better results than you are having right now. In fact I am surprised that you are having as good results as you are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Everybody is out of step but "Our Willie."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have not seen any great contribution made by the Conservative party when my hon. friend, the member for York-Sunbury was the leader. In fact I have not heard him make much of a contribution to the house since he has been here. He may have at times. I do not mean to belittle the hon. gentleman; but I would not do that. I think he has been doing his best; but you see where his best has landed us, because his best on the mobilization problem was exactly the same as the Liberal party's best. They were both in accord. Well do I remember seeing the late Doctor Manion rising in his place in this house and patting the government on the back for the policy they were pursuing in regard to the raising of man-power for this war. I will say that there were some members of the Liberal cabinet who objected to the practice being used then, and are no doubt objecting now, but they are not getting very far with it.
When I see the method being used to get the boys out of the defence army into the active army I think it is nothing short of shameful. If I were the government I would be absolutely ashamed to have any officer

War Appropriation-Labour
in the active army go out to intimidate or coerce these men who have complied in every degree with the government's request and have joined the defence army. They are trying to coerce or shame them into going active.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They are good and ashamed too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If they are not, they should be. The government should get out and speak to some of these boys in the defence army. You do not need to think for one minute that all these boys in the defence army are yellow; they are not by any manner of means. I have had them tell me this, and I think they are quite justified in the stand they take. They say: We joined the defence army because that was the government's policy and they asked us to do so. They sent us a call and we complied with it. We have joined the defence army, and we will join the active army when the government makes that their policy so that everybody has to go. Instead of that the government has agreed with army officers who go out and speak to the defence army in the way in which Major General Pearkes did the other day.
May I quote from the Canadian Veteran of April 30, 1944? This is what Major General Pearkes is reported to have said:
Major General G. R. Pearkes, V.C., general officer commanding-in-chief, Pacific command, in an address to a group of soldiers at Vernon, B.C., training camp recently said:	"Cease
wavering, play the man's part, and join the active army of Canada."
What kind of language is that to use to men in the defence forces who have complied with the government's regulation and the government's policy? That language should be addressed to the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister. The article goes on:
General Pearkes said later: "I tried principally to appeal to their pride in Canada."
Why appeal to their pride? Why not appeal to the pride of the government? They were the ones who put this policy into operation. They were the ones who asked these boys to join the defence army. Why take it out on these boys? The government sends out officers to tell these boys they should be ashamed of themselves to be in the defence army of Canada. What kind of hypocrisy is that? Then the article goes on to say:
. . . and to the fact that the outcome of the second front might rest upon the number of home defence men who are ready to back up the troops already overseas.
What is the import of that statement? He says that the very existence of our Dominion of Canada may depend upon the willingness of the defence army to go active. Those words
should be applied to the government of this country and never to a man in uniform in the defence army.
Where are we to get the men for our active army ? As the Minister of Labour pointed out, he was cautioned by the Minister of National Defence that there was a great danger of our not getting enough men for the active army. It is the job of the Minister of Labour to see to it that these men are forced into the defence army, and forced from there into the active army. Can one find anything more despicable than that? It is almost subversive; I think it is. We have young men in industry or in agriculture receiving calls. They have to go before the selective service board, and the very first thing the selective service board asks them is: "Why are you not in the army?" Or they send them to some job to which the boys do not want to go, and they say: " If you do not go we will push you into the army." That was done in the selective service office in Calgary and I brought it to the attention of the minister. When they are in the defence army, by using that method we then send honourable gentlemen, worthy army officers who have served their country overseas, among these men, and we put the shameful task on such officers of going out to these men who have complied in every way with the government's law and the government's regulations, to induce them to join the active army.

speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. member who has had the, floor up to this time this evening has, I submit, totally, wilfully and knowingly misrepresented my position on the question of national selective service. I desire to call the attention of this committee and the country to the amendment which I moved in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne on January 26, 1942. In that debate I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Yale, the following amendment to the motion then before the house:
This house regrets _ that Your Excellency's advisers, instead of giving to the country the leadership so essential at a time properly described in the speech from the throne as the greatest crisis in the world's history, on the contrary, have sought to evade their responsibility by holding a plebiscite, which, in the view of this house, is the negation of responsible government.
And this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have not seen fit to recommend to parliament without delay additional measures designed to
War Appropriation-Labour

(a)	completely mobilize the wealth and material resources and, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation, to the end that the nation may wage total war in any theatre of war;
(b)	supply the imperative needs of agriculture, industry and the fighting forces of the nation; and
(c)	prepare for the post-war period.
I call upon the hon. member to recall the statements he made with respect to myself, deliberately, falsely, ignorantly and, I say, maliciously.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to get some information from the minister in regard to naval personnel. Naval general order No. 3098, entitled "discharge for return to essential industry or to agriculture," has this to say in paragraph 5:
A notation is to be made on t'he service certificate of any rating discharged under this order to the effect that he is discharged "at own request to return to essential industry or to agriculture," as applicable. The Department of Labour have given assurance that selective service mobilization 'boards will grant deferment from army call-up to persons who present service certificates so inscribed, until such time as t'he circumstances which warranted discharge have altered materially.
We have these young men who have been in the navy for some considerable time, perhaps a year or more, and have been trained at the expense of the nation. For some reason or another they are discharged at their own request, perhaps following the death of the father, and they return to civilian life. But in paragraph 6B, page 7 of "Canadian War Orders and Regulations" dated March 4, 1944, I read this:
1. When a registrar receives a notice in prescribed form from a representative of the Department of National Defence that a designated man has ceased or will soon cease to -be a member of His Majesty's Canadian naval or air forces on active service and is considered fit for military training, the registrar may, whether the man resides in the registrar's division or not, serve him or cause him to be served, either personally or by registered post, *with an order, in prescribed form, requiring him to report at a military centre, at a time and place indicated therein, to be dealt with in accordance with the orders and regulations of,

War Appropriation-Labour
or relating to the Department of National Defence, and any man to whom an "order-military training" is sent under this subsection shall comply therewith and shall submit to the medical examination for which provision is made in the National Resources Mobilization Act (army) regulations, 1943.
2. Where an "order-military training" has been served pursuant to this section, the provisions' of these regulations shall apply mutatis mutandis as if it had been served pursuant to section six.
Here you have a man who has served in the navy for perhaps twelve months and has been trained as a stoker or a seaman. He returns to take his place on the farm, as authorized by the naval department. Then he is immediately called up; the man who has been a volunteer becomes a conscript and is taken into the army. I want the minister to look into this matter and straighten it up. I consider it very unfair that a man who volunteered but who, because of conditions recognized by the navy, has been allowed to return to the farm, should be called up again by the war services board and put into the army as a conscript.

speechtext:
I can assure the minister that it does exist, and I shall be pleased to let him have further information.
Then on Friday evening the minister referred to the packing industry, which he said was employing twice as many people as in 1939. That is quite reasonable, because in 1939 we killed 5,389,000 animals, while in 1943 we killed 8,572,000, an increase of sixty per cent In addition, we must remember that more women and more unskilled labour are being employed. I should like to impress upon the minister that the packing plants require the 100-159
extra ten per cent of man-power at this time. It is estimated that the weekly run of hogs will be 140,000 for the next six weeks, and the packing plants have not the people to kill them. This means that the farmers will have to take it in the neck again; the hogs will be sent from Edmonton right through to Toronto to be killed, and there is a tremendous shrinkage when that trip has to be made. According to the Department of Agriculture the weekly run of cattle will be 16,200, and the plants will be able to kill only 13,800 with the men they now employ. If you could give them ten per cent more help they could always work a few hours extra and cope with the situation. Will the minister be good enough to look into that matter, because it means a great deal to the farmers of the west? If cattle and hogs have to be shipped from Edmonton and Calgary to Toronto for killing, the loss through shrinkage is tremendous.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think it is some achievement that we have been able to double the number of employees in the packing plants of this country. I am not trying to wish myself out of a difficult position; there are not enough men and women in our packing plants, particularly in western Canada. I know something of the contribution made by the farmers of that part of Canada, and we are well aware of this condition. I think it can be truthfully said, notwithstanding some of the expressions of opinion here this evening, that we oi selective service have measured up to our responsibilities. As I said this afternoon, the man-power of this country is organized as well as or better than in any other of the united nations with the exception of Great Britain. Let those people who sit behind editorial desks in some of the larger centres of this dominion repeat that statement, if they will. We are alive to this situation in western Canada. We are doing everything humanly possible to meet the labour requirements of the packing industry there. Only to-day meetings were held in Winnipeg, Regina and Edmonton, and I feel confident we can put the necessary man-power into the packing industry in that part of the country within the next two weeks.
Perhaps I should not say this, but I have no control over the number of cattle or pigs bom in this country every year. I was not there when that was decided, and you cannot blame selective service for it. But once the fact exists, and we are conscious of it, we can move man-power into the packing plants to do the necessary slaughtering and to make preparation either for consumption in the home market or for shipment overseas.

War Appropriation-Labour

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question somewhat similar to that asked by the hon. member for Selkirk. I have had drawn to my attention a number of cases respecting men who have served overseas, in some cases for several years, and who, upon being returned to Canada and being discharged because of medical unfitness, have been called up by local mobilization boards. I am not certain whether these are mistakes, or form part of the government's policy. It is done, apparently, with the full knowledge that these men have served overseas, because a letter I have received from the Canadian Legion states:
Whoever is in charge of the calling up in this city is taking a very dictatorial attitude by calling these men up, and when it is pointed out that these men have already served, simply remark, "We do as we please."
So that it is not done in ignorance, when these men are called up. The mobilization board must know full well that they have served overseas.
One case brought to my attention concerns a man who was discharged as recently as April 3. Now he is called by selective service. I am asking the minister to clarify this situation. I understand that in January of this year regulations were passed which, in effect, excuse a man with overseas service from being called up. I have in mind a man named Coyle who, apparently, has been released again. Apparently when the matter was referred by selective service to the Department of National Defence, that department took the attitude that they did not want to have the man called up. Is that just one isolated case, or will that apply in regard to all men who have served overseas? What is the general policy?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
First of all may I offer an apology to the hon. member for Selkirk. I spoke loudly only so that he could hear; I was not being critical.
We do what the hon. member for Acadia has suggested, namely, make reexaminations. Men who are discharged from the navy for seasickness-and there are some cases of that kind-are quite capable of serving in the army. With the exception of crossing the ocean on a transport, the soldier does not 
have much opportunity for seasickness. I have suffered from seasickness, and I do not treat the matter lightly.
Then there are cases of colour-blindness of men at sea or in the air, where it is necessary that they should not be colour-blind. Anyone with any knowledge of the sea will understand the reason for that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Are those exceptions? I
am more interested in the men who, after having served oVerseas probably for a number of years, are discharged because of medical unfitness, not because of colour-blindness or seasickness. They are discharged because their health has deteriorated on account of overseas service. I think it is very wrong that men who have seen overseas service should now be drafted. These men have a real right to feel that they suffer a grievance against the country. Surely after a man has volunteered to serve, has served for three years overseas and has been discharged on account of his health, he should not be drafted. It is something we should be thoroughly ashamed of, and certainly it should not be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
To be perfectly frank,
these men are designated by the military authorities, and we do the examining. It is quite true that we have reached almost the bottom of the man-power barrel, so far as able-bodied men are concerned. As I said before, we have to examine six in order to get one man for the armed forces; that is the position we are in at the present time. There are some who say that there is almost total mobilization in Canada. When we reach that position I think we have reached a position on a par with almost any country in the united nations groups. That is the position we find ourselves in to-day, namely, that we have to examine six men to get one for the services.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Where this policy has to be carried out, I wonder if it still would not be possible to do something to take care of ' two kinds of grievances of which I happen to know. I have in mind a case into which, in response to my request, the minister's deputy is examining. I dare to hope that it may be taken care of. The case is that of a young man who had served three years and seven months in the air force and was discharged as being medically unfit for further service in the air force. I was permitted to look into his file by one of the senior officers, and I discovered that while his medical condition upon discharge was such that he could not continue in the air force, still it was clear that he could be of some use in the army. The young man did not object to going into the army, but he had two grievances. The first was that he would now be a conscript, despite

War Appropriation-Labour
the fact that he had served as a volunteer for three years and seven months. His second grievance was that, although upon being discharged from the air force he held the rank of sergeant, upon entering the army he would have to start again at the bottom.
Is there anything that can be done about these two grievances? The information I have received confirms what the minister has said, namely, that it is a matter of policy. I was told by an officer in the air force, with whom I was in contact, that when the air force discharges a man as being medically unfit selective service is notified and, in most instances, these men are handed their call-up slips at the time they are given their discharge papers. Can these grievances be looked into?

speechtext: I shall be glad to do that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister some questions in connection with national selective service. My questions are based upon two paragraphs in the minister's speech of Friday last. At page 2431 of Hansard he is reported as follows:
Next is the national selective service administration board, over which the director of national selective service presides. This board is composed of the associate directors of national selective service and carries the burden of the day-to-day administrative problems. As members of the administration board are also members of the advisory board, coordination of advisory and administrative functions is as complete as possible.
Of course that is a very general statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Then, this is the important paragraph, and the one upon which I shall base the questions I shall ask the minister:
Decentralization has been provided for by the appointment of regional directors and regional national selective service advisory boards in Quebec, Ontario, the prairies and the Pacific. An advisory board for the maritimes will be constituted in due course.
I want to know why there has not been an advisory board appointed heretofore for the maritime provinces. I express this fear to the minister, that unless great care is taken, while war work is still going on actively in Canada- and that may be for the next two years-we are going to be denuded of our population down there. That would not be a good thing for the maritimes or for Canada. That is not decentralization; it is centralization. We must watch out to see that labour is not drawn off from the maritimes and other parts to the central provinces, where they may stay when the war is over and so denude us of our 100-159i
population. But that process is going on. I know, for instance, that the production of certain plants is being curtailed. I have one in mind at the moment, where the workers are being offered positions in upper Canada, and a good many of them are going. Is there any board whose function it is to watch that situation and see that too much of our population, perhaps a very fine part of our population, is not being depleted for the benefit of the central provinces?
The minister knows as well as I do that there is a tremendous cry in Canada, in the east and in the west, against so much centralization of industry in central'Canada. I do think that is a bad thing for the body politic. I would think there are a good many contributing factors. I know this, that geography, which we cannot overcome except by means that are perhaps uneconomic, has had a tendency to drain off our industries to central Canada. I remember discussing this very problem with the late A. 0. Dawson, who was for many years head of Canadian Cottons Limited. We have several cotton factories in New Brunswick, and all the raw material has to be brought in by rail. It comes up, I learned much to my surprise, all the way by rail from New Orleans in the south to Fredericton and Saint John and Milltown. I had thought that it would be brought by water, pre-war, but they tell me that that is not the case. Then, because we have such a limited population in the maritime provinces the finished product has to be sent back and marketed in central or western Canada. So that geography is distinctly against that industry in the maritimes.
I know that industries have a tendency to move to where the demand for their goods is, to where there is more money and more consumption. I have in mind a candy manufacturing establishment, very well known, producing a nationally known product. I am afraid that if that industry were damaged by fire or what-not, it would not be started up again in the maritime provinces but probably would be established in Toronto.
And hon. MEMBER: Is that Moir's?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I am not mentioning any particular firm. We all have our favourites; they are all good, and I am not here to advertise any nationally known product. The point I am making is that, so far as I know, national selective service has not yet set up any administrative board to take care of that situation and prevent what I fear may become quite a heavy drain of our population, denuding us perhaps of the very
War Appropriation-Labour

best part of our people. I should like to have some reassurance from the minister on that point because it is important.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I am a great believer in decentralization. I think it is the greatest stabilizer that one can have in a country as large as Canada, which in area is a continent in itself, not a country. Selective service, moving along in progressive stages, reached the point where we thought there should be a measure of decentralization, and so we are setting up five regional boards, one for the maritimes, one for Quebec, one for Ontario, one for the prairie provinces and one for British Columbia. These boards resemble the national board in make-up but have fewer representatives. They help to take the weight off the national selective service board, and by their familiarity with the peculiar problems of different parts of this dominion are able to have a bearing on the policies of the national board. We hope to set up such a board in the maritime provinces in the course of the next week.
Might I say to the hon. member for York-Sunbury that while there has been some movement of population from eastern Canada, there has also been a movement into the maritime provinces from other parts of Canada, and if one looked into the figures I think they would show that more people have moved into the maritimes than have left those provinces during the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Those
figures would be very interesting; I should like to see them. I know that a large population of women has been moved from the maritimes to Toronto.

speechtext: At Halifax and Truro-

speechtext: They are populated by an influx of the armed forces, the navy particularly.

I had in mind shipyards, which come directly under my jurisdiction, also the construction industry, and when you take these into account you will find that the balance is fairly even, as between the movement of labour from one part of the dominion to another.

Now- it so happened that many of the men and women working in that plant had come in there from
TMr. R. B. Hanson.]
upper Canada, as it is called in those parts, and in view of this clause in the agreement, many of the people first laid off were the local people, being the last ones taken on. I will not say what they called the workers from upper Canada who retained their jobs in Amherst.

speechtext: They did not call them out of their name, I hope.

I should like to pay a compliment to a very large body of workers in this country, the largest single body of workers in the country, namely, the railway men and women of Canada. In the wrangling that sometimes goes on in some parts of the country and amidst all the disturbances that sometimes arise, we are apt to forget the tremendous contribution which these railway men and women are making to Canada's war effort. They have had to overcome almost insurmountable odds in the way of lack of help and obsolete equipment such as I think no other body of men have had to face in this dominion. Everyone who travels the trains must realize the difficulties with which our railway men have to cope, and I think the patience, courtesy and restraint with which they go about their work is a remarkable example to the rest of Canada that might well be emulated by those who use the facilities which the railways provide. One of the reasons why in my opinion the railroads have been able to do the remarkable job they have

I wish to ask the minister a question, to make a short observation and then to give him a suggestion. I am not altogether satisfied that the selective service boards are turning out in the way in which they were first expected to operate. I am going to ask the minister to consider making the situation such that when men and women go to the selective service offices seeking employment they will have a certain amount of freedom. The picture as I see it is this. The employer has an opening for a man, perhaps in a store or an office. He applies to the selective service offices. I do not know what is done there, but a man who wants a position goes to the selective service offices. He does not know who his employer may be. The employer does not know whom he may have to employ. Instead of the selective service offices being a sort of clearing house to keep the records straight and attempt to supply and satisfy all industry and all employers, it becomes a sort of bureaucratic institution which has a tendency to push men here and there, and to push on to an employer perhaps somebody with whom he is not altogether satisfied. That is the picture as I see it, and I believe I am right in giving that picture.
I am reminded of what seemed to be the situation last fall. I bring this to the minister's attention, but I do not want him to think what I am about to say is all hearsay, because in this case I happen to know what I am talking about. Last fall the Royal Canadian Air Force put on a campaign to induce women to join the R.C.A.F. I know there was an attempt on one or two occasions by the selective service officials to persuade, very carefully and very cleverly, certain young women to join the R.C.A.E. when they went to the selective service boards looking for employment. I know that happened. I know what took place. The conversation goes along something like this: "What sort of work do you wish?" says the official. The reply is: "Well, I would like anything I can get. I am willing to work hard. I do not want to go out minding children, but I do not mind working in a store." The next question is: "Would you like a stenographer's job?" The answer is, "Well, I cannot do stenography." Then eventually the conversation gets down to the place where the official says, "Well, you know, if you join the forces you can get a job there, and they will teach you. They will train you and you can receive pay while you are training." I know that is what happened. I am not making any drastic accusations or anything of that kind, and I do not want to be unkind. But I should

like to know whether the duties of the selective service officer call for him to do that or whether he is to satisfy the employer and the person who is looking for employment. The thing seems to be a bit shrouded in mystery. A man or a woman goes into the office. They do not know what they are to get. They do not know what is open. They are not told what is open. They say, "I do this", or "I do that", or "I do something else". "I can do so many things. I should like to get employment". Then they are told where they should go. The same situation applies to the other side of the picture with the employer.
I suggest to the minister that when a man goes to the selective service offices there should be some way by which he can choose his position. I do not mean that the selective service officers should be turned into the oldtime labour office where men went and paid so much and saw all sorts of positions put up on big cards on the side of the wall somewhere; but I believe that the selective service officers should be more open in this respect. I suggest that there should be a bulletin board where all those positions that are open should be displayed so that a man could look them over and say to the selective service officers: "I can do this; I want to apply for this position." The employer's name should be displayed as well so that the man has some measure ' of freedom in seeking the work he wants to do. The employer should be able to put an advertisement in the paper. I do not mean that he should be allowed to handle the whole thing himself, although I would not be adverse to that. The individual could then apply through selective service for the position, giving the name of the firm, and as far as that goes, the individual could go to the firm and say, "I am looking for this job; am I competent?" They should be able to say: "Yes, we will take you; go and clear with the selective service officials."
I make this suggestion to the minister, namely, that all the positions that are open should be open to the observation of the men and the women who want the jobs, and that the employer should have some measure of freedom in choosing the man or the woman that he wants to employ. Would the minister give some consideration to that? I think it would tend to satisfy the employer and the employee, much more than the system does at present. I have always thought that water would find its own level; that is, nature, if it is left alone, will do very well. I think the same principle applies in a world of free men. I do not believe that you can begin to push men around, regiment them, put them here and

War Appropriation-Labour
there against their will, or against their knowledge, and expect the most harmonious relationship between employers and employees and the middleman, which is the selective service board.
I believe that the minister will find all kinds of trouble and criticism if there is not a little more freedom among employers and employees in relation to the selective service board. Would the minister give some consideration to having these positions either on a bulletin board or exhibited in some way so that men seeking employment would know where they could go and have some choice in the matter?

I appreciate the suggestions that my hon. friend has made, and while I am conscious that there is a measure of criticism of the Department of Labour and the minister, yet this is one of the few opportunities that the minister gets to meet his peers when we are discussing the policies in connection with the different departments of government. The first point raised by my hon. friend was that of the recruitment of women for the navy, the air force and the army. I want to be perfectly frank with him. This is the policy of the labour department. When France fell I was one of the strongest advocates of taking women into the fighting forces, because every woman you take in frees a man for a more active part in the three services. We are proud of the contribution that we have made to'the fighting forces through the instrumentality of selective service as a recruiting agency for the young women who have joined the three departments of our armed forces. It is absolutely voluntary. There is persuasion, it is true, but let me say very frankly that there is no coercion.
On the question of selective service, at the top we have what we call the national selective service advisory board on which are represented all the armed services, the prices control board, munitions and supply, labour, agriculture and the various employers' organizations. On any major question of high policy no move is made until this board is consulted. May I say this to the hon. gentleman, who is not in his seat at the present time: Those of us who take our minds back to twelve or eighteen months ago realize you cannot solve a problem by running away from it; you have to stay with the ship. No one appreciates more than those in the labour department the difficulties and complexities of organizing the measure of selective service that exists in this country to-day. We have had to issue plenty of shalls and do's and don'ts and won'ts; but I want to say to the committee-and this is in line with the thought of my hon. friendthat when this war is over I hope it will be said of me that nothing I did had the effect of impairing the fundamental principles of freedom that have made this country what it is to-day. We have passed through many difficulties, including the poaching of labour when employers were stealing the employees of other employers. I remember the questions asked in that connection in this house before I came into the ministry. The real core of our manpower policy is the control of man-power. I was in Philadelphia a week ago. I picked up the Sunday Inquirer and found seven pages of "help wanted" advertisements, which is an indication that they are passing through the same uncontrolled condition in regard to industrial, farm and commercial labour that we passed through two years ago. I want to say to the committee that without the controls we have in operation at the moment, such as the priority of industries and control over the movement of men and women, we would have complete chaos in Canada.
The fundamental fact we must keep in mind is that to-day the per capita production of this country is the largest of any nation in the world. Do not take my word for it; Madame Chiang Kai-shek made that observation right in this chamber when addressing members of the Commons and the Senate. That is the result not only of the genius of the Canadian people but also of the measure of labour control we have in this dominion. I want to pay a tribute to employers, employees and farmers, and to their various organizations. We sometimes like things to reflect to our own glory, but these results would not have been possible without the active cooperation of those forces in the life of this nation. I cannot and would not promise any hon. member-and goodness knows I get enough pressure from all directions-that there will be any slackening of these controls until the labour situation is much easier than it is at the moment. I remember that last fall certain members of this house went up and down the country saying there would be an unemployment situation in Canada this spring, with 100,000 people out of work. I do not know why they said those things, whether it was for political reasons or to embarrass the government, but in my judgment it does not reflect credit upon any responsible member of this house to express in public a thought of that kind when we are facing the most desperate hour in the history of this nation.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the comprehensive report the minister gave us the other evening, which contains very much that is extremely commendable. I was particularly interested in the features pertaining to education, and when those matters come up for review I shall have something further to say. This afternoon I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre. I am not nearly so disturbed about the increased purchase of civilian goods in 1944 in comparison with 1939 as the hon. member appears to be.
I think he loses sight of the fact that in 1939 large numbers of our people had been without purchasing power for many years. Now that they are in possession of some purchasing power it is only natural that they should spend part of it to acquire goods which they were forced by economic conditions to go without for many years prior to the war. The hon. member for Lake Centre also had a good deal to say about equality of service and sacrifice. On some occasion I should like the hon. gentleman or someone in his party to explain to the house just what they mean by that expression, which I have heard them use many times. Just what do they mean when they refer to equality of service as between different parts of the country or as between different classes within the country? I think 
it would avoid considerable confusion if we knew just what meaning they attach to the term.
In connection with selective service I should like to endorse the statement made on Friday evening by the hon. member for Cape Breton South as to the importance, in the selective service machinery, of those who make the first contact with people seeking employment. As the minister has just pointed out, it is very difficult to undertake to direct men from one industry to another, or to tell Canadians, who all their lives have been free to choose jobs to their own liking when they could get them, where they must work. I think a good deal of the criticism I have heard in regard to selective service arises from the lack of understanding and courtesy on the part of those who have the first interviews with people coming to selective service for positions. I realize that the minister has had to make use of untrained, unskilled people. Any effort that can be spent on training those people to make that first contact with the public, so that a man or woman who comes to discuss the question of a job with selective service is not given to feel that the selective service officer is looking down upon the unemployed person, would be worth while. Anything of that kind should be avoided, wherever possible.
As I have seen the long queues of unem-. ployed, or those seeking to transfer from one job to another, as I have seen them lined up in some of the Toronto offices, particularly on Spadina avenue, I have wondered if there is not some way of avoiding some of that complicated procedure which is followed. It seems to me that when a man registers with selective service, and selective service have his card on file, they must know what he is capable of doing, and what his experience and qualifications are. They have the whole case history on their cards, and it seems to me it should be possible for selective service, upon being ' notified by an employer that he wants a certain type of employee, to notify such employee who might be qualified for the job, and to instruct him to go directly to that job. It should not be necessary for him to make a trip, sometimes of many miles, to the selective service office, and stand in line possibly for hours-and in many cases have to go back more than once to make contact with the job. Even then, a person may be sent to a job that has been filled by the time he gets there. I am wondering if there cannot be some shortcut whereby some of that inconvenience .and annoyance may be avoided. Is it not possible to notify the employee direct as to where he may apply for a job for which he is fitted? Any study that can be given to that phase of the programme would help.

War Appropriation-Labour
I have noticed from time to time that there appears to be little coordination between different offices of selective service. A man comes into a selective service office, and they have nothing that fits his qualifications. They appear to have no record of vacancies which would suit him, but which might be on file in other offices. I recall, for instance, a graduate druggist going into a selective service office, and the only job the office could offer him was one in a lumber camp. They had not a single opening on their files for a graduate chemist. I am sure there were other offices that had on their files vacancies for a man with those qualifications. I am wondering just what coordination there is among different offices within selective service.
As I have moved from province to province I have noticed that there is considerable lack of uniformity, particularly in the manner of getting those men from industry, temporarily employed on farms, back into their original jobs, or back into industry. I find that in Ontario the practice appears to be that of sending a registered letter to the employer, a similar letter to the employee, and a registered letter to the farmer for whom he has been working. That appears to be a good deal of duplication and waste of time. An enormous number of clerks must be employed as stenographers to write those three letters and to register them. Yet all this must be done to get a man back from a temporary farm job into his original job in industry. It seems to me there should be some shorter cut to effect that transfer.
Then I am wondering what cooperation the minister and his department are getting from employers in the matter of lay-offs. I was in Amherst, Nova Scotia, when a considerable lay-off took place from the Canadian Car and Foundry company, and I discovered that the men were on the streets before selective service knew anything about the lay-off. I am wondering if the department is getting the cooperation to which it is entitled. Certainly employers can assist in this whole business by keeping selective service informed well in advance with respect to lay-offs about to take place, and also as to what their needs will be, in order that selective service may have an opportunity to fill those needs. I have heard selective service officers in different towns complain that often men were thrown upon them, from industry, without very much notification, and that demands were made upon them by industry without much advance notice.
Certainly the minister or his department cannot be blamed for that; but it is one feature in which this whole business of selective
service can be improved. I hear unofficially that the minister's department is now making a job survey across Canada. If that is so, I wish to commend the minister. It is something I am sure he should have done long ago, and something which is certainly most timely to-day. I would say simply this to the minister, that I have heard that those who are entrusted with this important task are greatly understaffed, and cannot be expected to make a really efficient survey, or to do an efficient job unless more assistance is given to them. In my opinion this is a very important job, and every possible cooperation and assistance should be given to those who are to undertake the task.
This afternoon I listened to the debate between the hon. member for Lake Centre and the minister with respect to all those missing men. ' I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre placed on record the estimated figure at 350,000. I believe the. figures showed by the minister's department are to blame for the conclusion reached by the hon. member. I am surprised, however, that he kept the figure down to 350,000. I have before me three returns tabled by the minister's department, and I can prove conclusively from those figures that there are at least 700,000 men missing.

I am not a statistician, but I can add and subtract figures. It can be shown conclusively from three separate sets of figures issued by the minister's department that there must be at least 700,000 men unaccounted for. That, of course, cannot be the fact. But the tables published by the minister's department justify one in reaching that conclusion. I wonder if the minister is not the victim of circumstances in this case. Probably he has inherited something there. I wonder if the minister or any other department of government has a record or whether there is a cross-check between the Department of National Defence and his department thar would show clearly just how many men of those called up had, prior to their call, or immediately upon their call, or between the time they were called and the time they were supposed to report, voluntarily enlisted. Without those figures one can only guess at how many men are unaccounted for. One cannot possibly estimate the number unless he has an accurate record. I should like to know if there is any such a record in the minister's department or in any other department, going back over the years.

I think that is a true statement. I want to make it quite clear that I have always taken every opportunity to assist recruiting for the three armed services. True enough, I may have been elected in 1940 as opposed to conscription. I made my stand very clear immediately upon the fall of France and other European countries; it will be found recorded in Hansard of November 10, 1941, at page 4210; and I have never veered from that stand at any time. I do not think we have national selective service in operation in this country yet.
Let me give the committee one or two examples. A young chap, a neighbour of mine, volunteered for service in the air force, hoping he would "make" the aircrew He did not make aircrew; he is now in groundcrew. He has clear title to a section of the best land in Manitoba, and it was a splendid farm. In recent months his father-in-law, who was operating the farm, has been told by his medical adviser that he cannot work any longer on the farm. This young chap thinks that, rather than be in groundcrew, he can render better service by operating that farm, but so far his efforts to get back to the farm have been fruitless.
I can take hon. members to another constituency over the border, in another province, and point out a somewhat similar case, a Y.C. of the Boer war who is farming, who has only one son, that son being in the armed services, and has been unable to get him out of the service to assist him on the farm. A farmer next to him has six sons of military age, all exempt upon the pretext of assisting in farm work, though the story the neighbours tell is to the effect that they are not making any great contribution to the war effort, either on the farm or anywhere else.
I give those two cases as concrete examples. If there is no coercion, no conscription in respect of this recruiting system for home defence, I wish to ask the Minister of

My understanding is that no young man is granted postponement or exemption unless he asks for it. I desire to make a very few observations, and the first one will be with respect to the order in which the items of this department are discussed. When, on February 11, the Minister of Finance introduced his resolution to provide for the sum of $3,650 millions, he made a break-down of the estimated war expenditure and indicated the order in which the various items should be discussed. I do not know why there has been this inversion of the order which was indicated by the Minister of Finance for the discussion of the estimates. Is it because the minister wanted to pass his estimate on a Friday evening or on a Monday? To-day we were supplied with a sheet showing a statement of estimated amounts required by the Department of Labour, and instead of having as the first item, as indicated by the Minister of Finance, the war emergency training programme, we find the national selective service programme. I am at a loss to know why this change has been made. The leader of the opposition has time and again complained about not knowing what was going on, what was to be discussed after we come here. We do not know what discussion will take place or what the order will be. In this case the minister has seen fit to change the order indicated, which we were entitled to believe would be adhered to. Moreover, we were supplied this afternoon with a statement printed in English only. I asked for a French copy of it but I was told there was none. The French language has a right in this house, and I am one of those who believe that, if it has, it is high time we were entitled to a French copy of everything printed. Last week we were discussing amendments to the standing orders of the house and were supplied only with an English copy. An hon. member opposite asked for a French copy and could not get it and to-day again we cannot get a French copy. We have only an

War Appropriation-Labour
English copy, which is different, as indicated on February 11 by the Minister of Finance.
And now I intend to continue my observations in French.
(Translation):	I wish to bring to the
attention of the committee the obviously absurd manner in which the provisions of the mobilization act are carried out. I do not know whether conditions are the same in the other provinces, but such is the situation in the province of Quebec. On February 8, 1943, *the minister sent us a copy of some directions given in connection with the growing shortage of farm labour. Here is one passage which I wish to quote:
Owing to the growing shortage of farm labour, it becomes increasingly important to encourage essential farm workers to remain on the land.
That is the direction which the Minister of Labour was giving with a view to keeping farm labour on the land. Unfortunately, those instructions were not followed, and I am going to give many examples. The other day, during the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), I brought some facts to his attention and he referred me to the Minister of Mobilization, adding that all he has to do is to ask the Minister of Mobilization for a certain number of recruits, and he undertakes to call them.
Well, it has happened many times that a farmer who had already been examined and placed in category E, and who was accordingly unfit for military service, was called again for a new medical examination in Montreal. The other day, the Minister of National Defence pointed out that it may sometimes be important that a new examination be made of recruits or of men liable to be called.
That was the case of a farmer who had already been called for medical examination and who, therefore, had applied for postponement as a farmer. The Department of Mobilization was aware of all the facts; they knew that the man was a farmer, that as a result of the first medical examination he had been put in category E, but they were calling him again for a new medical examination, at the very time when farmers were requested to remain on their farms. And I could mention several cases. There is, for instance, the case of a young married man who owned a 160-acre farm which he operated alone. He had to lose one or two days to undergo a new medical examination in Montreal and during his absence his neighbours had to take care of his herd of cows. That was an unnecessary expense, in the first place, and a loss of time for that farmer.
I would ask the minister to tell us how many farmers have been called for a second
medical examination. I would ask him when opportunity allows, to kindly give me this information, and to tell me the cost of this second examination of farmers in the circumstances I have just mentioned. There are also other cases. A number of men were called for medical examination and although they applied for a postponement, they were ordered to report to a military training camp two or three days after undergoing the examination. This was a violation of the mobilization regulation which reads as follows:
T'he registrar shall not, while an application for a postponement order is pending before the board, send the applicant an "order-military training."
After submitting to the medical examination,, the applicant had fourteen days in which to apply for a postponement, and he had done so. And there is a large number of similar cases. I do not claim, however, that all this was done since the present minister is in charge of the department. However, I have in my files numerous cases where a called-up man who had applied for a postponement two or three days after receiving the first notice, received an "Order-Military Training". What was the consequence? A good many farmers went to training camps, under the impression that their request for a postponement had been rejected. And it took not only days and weeks, but often months to get them out of the camps after they had proved that they were farmers' sons and were entitled to deferments. During that time farms were neglected.
I recall the case of a 72 year old farmer, whose only son was railed up. The old man was left alone to look after the farm and a herd of dairy cows. The son's postponement *was not granted and he had to go to a training camp, where he had to stay for months before being released. The neighbours had to tend the cows and look after the other farm work. Farmers are asked to increase production; rationing has been resorted to; a shortage of farm help is being experienced; crops are rotting on the field and, nevertheless, farmers' sons are still being called up. Last week, a creamery operator who processes the cream of the farmers of the township, and -who makes butter for which there is such an acute need, saw with great dismay his buttermaker called up for a medical examination although he had been given a postponement until next July. Can anyone imagine such a way of carrying out the provisions of the act? That man had been granted a postponement until July and he -was called for a new medical examination. He was kept away from his farm during three
War Appropriation-Labour

days, and meanwhile there was an accumulation of cream because no one there could make his butter.
And what about the recruits who are called and who suffer from tuberculosis. The following question was recently asked:
How many members of the armed forces on duty in Canada only have been discharged on account of tuberculosis of the lungs?
The answer was that 2,489 persons had been discharged from the army because they were suffering from, tuberculosis. And it was further stated:
Most of the cases had the disease on enlistment and were discharged as soon as the result of the X-ray plates was known.
How is it that they had been accepted in the army if they were suffering from tuberculosis? 2,489 men were suffering with this disease and were nevertheless kept in the armed forces, thereby exposing the others to possible contamination. Had ordinary care been taken, this would not have happened. I shall say nothing of the expense this represented for the taxpayers who always pay the bill in the end.
In spite of statements to the effect that fewer men are required, within Canada, for the defence of the country, more men are being called. I asked a question from the minister last March and, on the 27th of that month, he gave me his reply. Here is my question:
How many persons were called for their medical examination under the mobilization act, (a) during the month of January, 1944; (b) during the month of February, 1944; (c) from March 1 to March 15, 1944?
The answer was:
January, 1944, 26,007; February, 1944, 23,119; March 1-15, 1944, 8,174.
To a second question worded as follows:
How many persons received a notice to report 'or military training under the mobilization act, (a) during the month of January, 1944; fb) during the month of February, 1944; (c) from March 1 to March 15, 1944?
The following answer was given:
January. 1944, 14.766; February, 1944, 12,172; March 1-15, 1944, 6,950.
And it is stated that fewer men are required within Canada, for the defence of the country. Well, let us stop fooling the public by insinuating that the men called for defence of Canada within Canada are really brought into the army for this purpose. It is to train recruits for overseas service, as the minister admitted the other day. It is a method of disguised conscription for overseas.
I come now to the order issued a few weeks ago by the Minister of Labour and which

compels every employer to report his employees who might not be complying with the Mobilization Act. This order even compels the father to report his son, the brother his brother, under penalty of a fine or imprisonment.
Male employee comprises any man in your employ, including those related to you.
And in a set of instructions, later supplied to employers, the same definition appears:
The expression "employer" also comprises any farmer operating a farm and who has a male employee even if he be his son or a relative.
I state without hesitation that, in this order the government is resorting to methods unworthy of a civilized country. To my mind, nothing is more inhuman, more antisocial than to compel parents to denounce their own children. In the name of the mogt elementary principles of justice and charity, I ask the government to remove this shameful order from our statutes. In this, I simply echo the numerous protests that have come from all parts of the country. All our public bodies have expressed their disapproval. In spite of all this, such an order is maintained.
I also wish to call the ministers' attention to order in council C.P. 1355, of March 4, 1940, which reads as follows:
The minister, upon 'being informed by the Department of National Defence that a specified number of men are required for military training, may instruct any registrar to apply these regulations to a specified number of _ men from his division, and may inform a registrar how many French-speaking men are required.
I ask the minister why he has inserted in this order in council a special provision relating to French-speaking Canadians. I thought that in this country of ours we were all Canadians and that when men are called into [DOT]the army there should be no distinction between French Canadians or English Canadians or Canadians of any other race, because we are all Canadians. I fail to see the object of this special distinction applying to French Canadians. As long as the Minister of Labour has not given a satisfactory explanation, I shall take it that this provision has been aimed at the French Canadians.
I shall have other remarks to make on this department's estimates. For the present, I call the minister's attention to he facts I have indicated to [DOT] the house, in the hope that he will give them due consideration and that he will take steps to remedy the difficulties I have mentioned.

"all a young man has to do when called up is to say that he is engaged in agriculture and he is automatically granted a postponement." The minister is entirely wrong. In practice the onus of proof at all times falls upon the man applying for postponement. I should like to tell the minister also that even many of those who have been granted postponements are advised from time to time that their postponements are cancelled, and that they must make new applications if they wish their cases reconsidered. In most of these cases conditions have not changed; yet the men are told that their postponements cannot be extended indefinitely. Why, then, should the minister make the statement in the house that agricultural postponements are readily granted when applied for, when he should know that such is not the case?
The point I wish to stress is that we know that men are needed for the armed services and that pressure is being applied to obtain men engaged in agriculture. They are told that their postponements cannot be carried on indefinitely and that sooner or later they will have to report for duty. We should be frank about the situation and state it in clear terms. The man-power policy of the government is that if a mobilization board finds that a man can be persuaded to enter the armed services, everything possible is done to get him to do so, even though he may be absolutely necessary on the farm. He cannot obtain his postponement unless and until he can prove beyond doubt that his parents could not possibly carry on without him. Statements like the one the minister made do not clarify the situation. When touring my constituency I was asked by many of my constituents, "Why does the government continue to announce over the air and in the press that postponements are being granted, while applications for postponement are in many cases flatly refused?" I think the minister should tell the house and the country that our man-power pool is being exhausted, and that pressure is being applied to get as many men as possible for the armed services, wherever they may be obtained.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with the reinstatement of returned men, those getting their positions back upon discharge. I imagine that would come under this item. They return to their jobs, and to positions not worse than they would have had, if they had not enlisted. What is done about that? Is there anything done so that these men are put back in jobs not worse than they would have had, had they not enlisted?
I have several cases here about which I wish to make some inquiry. I do not intend to mention names, but I would point out one or two cases in point. Here is one case-and there is a series of them. I think in some cases there is a lot of buck-passing in connection with taking these men back, and that is very bad for morale in the factories. If anyone should have consideration, certainly it should be those men who have been overseas and are returned again to civil life.
Here is one example. Before enlistment this man was a lead hand in a sheet metal department, and was receiving seventy-five cents an hour. He was wounded at Dieppe, and was discharged on April 3, 1944. Upon application for reinstatement he was told that there

were no vacancies. He was later reinstated in the sheet metal department at the rate of seventy-five cents an hour. A good deal of kicking went on. That amount included cost of living bonus. This man has the right at the present time to a wage of eighty-five cents.
Here is another case. This man was employed in September, 1941; enlisted in August, 1942; was discharged in February, 1944, and was reinstated at fifty-five cents an hour as a junior store clerk. The rate is still fifty-five cents, plus cost of living bonus. Employees who started after him are now receiving ninety cents an hour. They are all lead hands.
Those are just a couple of cases, but there are a great many others I could place on record. Could the minister explain just what is being done to see that men who are returned are getting their rights upon reinstatement, according to the laws of the land?

speechtext: Obviously I do not know the details of the cases to which the hon. member has referred. One cannot get down to individual cases in committee, because we are dealing with tens of thousands of men. But we have veteran welfare officers in all the larger centres of the dominion, and it seems to me that if these men have proper cases- and I think they are informed of that fact when they leave the army-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I might say that these cases have been given to me by the man who represents the legion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We do not know anything about them. We have welfare officers, and the law is clear in the matter. I understand that when these men leave the forces or are discharged they are informed as to their rights, and the machinery that exists for the assistance of men who have served in the fighting forces. Obviously on the floor of the house I cannot say what the facts are in connection with the cases my hon. friend has mentioned. However, of course I appreciate his having brought these to my attention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think the minister has understood me correctly. I brought up these cases only as examples.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I appreciate that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I want to know what the department is doing in matters of this kind-because these are only two; there are lots of others, and in various places. There is the greatest difficulty in some cases in connection with having these men reinstated in their position, or in a position which would not

be worse than they would have had, had they not enlisted. It is all very well to put them back into their jobs, but they must be not worse than they would have been, had they not enlisted. That is my point, and I think it is a serious matter.

speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that the mere fact that something is written on a piece of paper does not mean that such alleged facts are as set out. It does not mean that an investigation might not show the facts otherwise. However, if the hon. member will be good enough to turn the correspondence over to myself or to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I shall be glad to look into the facts.
